points: **Invitations:** Sch. 1A, Pt 1 treats inviting or inducing a person to enter a contract, or to make a material decision, as a regulated activity. Banners, push messages and ads aimed at customers can fall within it.

**Notice and consent:** PDPO s.35C requires notice of the intended use and a free channel to consent before personal data is used in direct marketing. Breach is an offence, with a fine of HK$500,000 and 3 years' imprisonment.
**Express consent:** s.35E(1) bars use without consent that matches the notified data and marketing classes. Oral consent needs written confirmation within 14 days. Breach carries the same penalty.

**Gifts and rebates:** GL25 bars gifts for Class C products and allows premium rebates on long-term products only where the rebate meets its criteria, including being recorded in the policy documents. Read GL25 before any promotion.
deepDive.takeaway: Treat every promotion as a regulated invitation with its own consent and record, not as marketing copy.

provisions.title: Conduct requirements for licensed insurance intermediaries
provisions.summary: When carrying on a regulated activity, a licensed insurance intermediary must act honestly and fairly in the customer's best interests, take care and skill, advise only within competence, consider the customer's circumstances, disclose what the customer needs to decide, avoid or disclose conflicts, and account promptly for the customer's assets.
provisions.counselNote: This is the core conduct duty for an agency in the app. It applies whatever the sales label, so every screen that arranges or invites a sale needs a conduct check.

provisions.title: Restrictions on carrying on regulated activities
provisions.summary: Cap. 41, s.64G(1) bars carrying on a regulated activity in the course of business or for reward. s.64G(3) carves out several licensed roles: an agency or individual agent acting for its appointing insurer, a broker company acting for policy holders, and technical representatives acting for the agency or broker that appointed them ((3)(a) to (e)). Contravention is an offence (s.64G(4)).
provisions.counselNote: This is the core licensing bar, and it limits which bank staff may sell or promote in the app. Map those roles before launch.

provisions.title: Regulated Activity, Material Decision and Regulated Advice
provisions.summary: Schedule 1A defines the acts that are regulated activities: negotiating or arranging a contract, inviting or inducing a person to enter a contract or make a material decision, and giving regulated advice. Part 2 lists material decisions and Part 3 lists regulated advice, both covering application, issue, renewal, change and claims.
provisions.counselNote: Inviting or inducing a purchase is caught as well as the sale itself, so banners, push messages and comparison features fall within the regime.

provisions.title: Contracts of insurance made through persons other than licensed insurance intermediaries, etc.
provisions.summary: An authorized insurer must not contract through, or accept a referral from, a person in Hong Kong unless that person is a licensed agency, an appointed licensed individual agent, a licensed broker company, or has clerical or administrative duties only. A contract made in breach can be enforced by, or voided at the option of, the policy holder.
provisions.counselNote: This limits who the insurer can use to reach customers in the app. Any partner that arranges, refers or takes applications must fit one of these categories.

provisions.title: Codes of conduct for licensed insurance intermediaries
provisions.summary: The IA may publish codes of conduct giving guidance on practices and standards for licensed intermediaries. A code may require continuing training. Breach of a code does not by itself create liability, but it can count against fitness to remain licensed, and a court must consider it where relevant.
provisions.counselNote: The codes are not a safe harbour. Compliance with a code is evidence the IA and courts will weigh, so the app's sales process should be checked against the agents' code.

provisions.instrument: Code of Conduct for Licensed Insurance Agents
provisions.title: Code of Conduct for Licensed Insurance Agents
provisions.summary: Issued under s.95 by the IA, the code sets practices and standards for licensed agents, covering conduct towards clients, disclosure, conflicts and complaints, with continuing training. Its exact paragraphs should be checked against the current edition.
provisions.counselNote: Map each sales screen to the code's conduct themes before launch. Check the current edition on the IA site, since the code can be amended under s.95(4).

provisions.instrument: IA Guideline on Financial Needs Analysis (GL30)
provisions.title: Financial needs analysis
provisions.summary: GL30 requires intermediaries to carry out a financial needs analysis before recommending a policy. Its scope, including which products it covers, should be confirmed against the current text. Its own text says it does not have the force of law. The Interpretation Notes (version 8, dated 26 August 2020) are in FAQ form.
provisions.counselNote: Build the needs analysis into the app before any recommendation, and keep the answers as the record for the suitability decision. Confirm the current operative paragraphs before go-live.

provisions.title: Cooling-off period
provisions.summary: GL29 gives a 21 calendar day cooling-off period, from delivery of the policy or a cooling-off notice, whichever is earlier, during which the policy holder can cancel and get a premium refund. It covers certain types of life insurance policies (its para 4.2 lists them; check the current text), so general cover follows each policy's own cancellation terms. Some products carry 30 days. It is a guideline under s.133, not law in itself.
provisions.counselNote: Set the cooling-off period from each product's terms and record the delivery date, since the clock depends on it. For general cover, check each policy's own cancellation terms.

provisions.title: Payment of prescribed levies
provisions.summary: The policy holder owes the levy to the IA (Cap. 41 s.134(1)) and must pay it to the insurer each time a premium is paid (s.3(1)). An intermediary that collects it must forward it to the insurer as soon as practicable, and the insurer must not keep any excess (s.3(2), (3)). The insurer remits it to the IA (s.4).
provisions.counselNote: The levy is part of the premium flow the app must show and collect. Agree with the insurer how each levy is collected and remitted to the IA, and read s.3(2) before relying on it.

provisions.title: Electronic signatures, digital signatures, etc.
provisions.summary: Where a rule of law requires a signature on a document, an electronic signature satisfies it if the signer uses a method that identifies him and shows approval, the method is reliable and appropriate for the purpose, and the other party consents to the method. Special rules apply where a government entity is involved.
provisions.counselNote: An in-app signature needs a method that is reliable for the purpose and the customer's consent to it. Record both, since they are what the bank will rely on if the signature is challenged.

provisions.title: Data user to take specified action before using personal data in direct marketing
provisions.summary: Before using personal data in direct marketing, the data user must tell the data subject of the intended use and that consent is needed, give the kinds of data and marketing classes, and provide a free channel to consent. Breach is an offence with a fine of HK$500,000 and 3 years' imprisonment.
provisions.counselNote: Any in-app marketing that uses customer data needs this notice and a consent channel before the first message. This is a criminal exposure, so build it into the consent flow.

provisions.title: Data user must not use personal data in direct marketing without data subject’s consent
provisions.summary: A data user may use personal data in direct marketing only with the data subject's consent to the intended use, within the permitted kinds of data and marketing classes. Oral consent needs written confirmation within 14 days. Breach is an offence with the same fine and imprisonment as s.35C.
provisions.counselNote: Consent must match the notified use. A later campaign outside the permitted classes needs fresh consent, so the consent record should store the scope, not only a yes or no.

provisions.title: Application of section 64G in relation to marketing insurance services outside Hong Kong
provisions.summary: A person who actively markets insurance services to the public from outside Hong Kong is treated as holding out that it carries on a regulated activity, whether it markets the services itself or through someone else.
provisions.counselNote: An app or campaign aimed at overseas or mainland customers can be treated as holding out under s.64G(2), even without a Hong Kong office. Review the target audience before any overseas marketing.

checklist: **Channel check:** Confirm the licensed route under s.64N(1) before any product goes live in the app.
**Class map:** Map each product to its Sch. 1 class, any certification (VHIS, QDAP) and any SFC authorization (ILAS).
**Regulated-activity map:** List every screen that invites, recommends or arranges a sale under Sch. 1A.
**Needs analysis:** Build a GL30 needs analysis step for each product family that needs one, and keep the answers.
**Disclosure set:** Agree the key facts, capacity, commission and conflicts disclosure needed under s.90(e) to (g).
**Cooling-off:** Record the delivery date and set the cooling-off period from each product's terms, using GL29 for certain life policies.
**Consent:** Capture PDPO s.35E consent before any direct marketing, with written confirmation if the consent was oral.
**Eligibility and records:** Set rules for special customers and keep the evidence trail for each sale.
itAngle: **E-signature:** Use a method that is reliable for the purpose and that the customer consents to (ETO s.6(1)). Log the method and the consent with each application.
**Screen-level rules:** Build conduct checks into each product screen, not only into the policy wording.
**Consent store:** Keep PDPO consents in a store the marketing system reads, with the date, the permitted data and the permitted marketing classes.
**Cooling-off timer:** Start the clock from the recorded delivery date and show the cancellation route inside the app.
bankNotes: **Authorized institution:** The IA has delegated its inspection and investigation powers over authorized institutions' insurance business to the Monetary Authority, a delegation in place since 23 September 2019 (s.4G; reported in IA and HKMA releases). The IA can still act itself (s.4G(5)), and it must consult the Monetary Authority before investigating or disciplining a bank (ss.64ZZH(2), 82(4), 84(4)).

**Two regulators:** The IA licenses and disciplines the bank and its people, and regulates how insurance is sold. Under the s.4G delegation the HKMA, as Monetary Authority, inspects and investigates the bank's insurance business and supervises the bank as a whole. Agree a single contact point for each.

**Referral risk:** The IA's 2019 explanatory note for banks treats a referral as a regulated activity where the bank steers a customer to a specific intermediary or earns remuneration for it (reported; check).
**Premium financing:** Where the bank also lends for premiums, it can act as both intermediary and financier, which the HKMA and IA circulars address separately.
pitfalls: **Labels:** Calling a product non-advised does not remove the s.90 duties from the agency.
**Promotions:** A banner that invites a purchase is a regulated activity, even if the bank is not the seller.
**Cooling-off:** GL29 covers certain life policies only, so do not apply its 21 days to every product. For general cover, check each policy's own cancellation terms.
**Consent:** Oral consent without written confirmation within 14 days breaches s.35E(1)(b).

glossary.definition: An act listed in Sch. 1A, Pt 1 of Cap. 41, such as arranging a contract, inviting a person to buy, or giving regulated advice. Doing one brings the intermediary within the conduct regime.
An opinion given on a matter listed in Sch. 1A, Pt 3, such as whether to apply for, change, or surrender a policy. A recommendation is an example.
A decision on a matter listed in Sch. 1A, Pt 2, such as applying for a policy, cancelling it, or making a claim.

A set number of days after delivery of a policy during which the policy holder can cancel and get a premium refund. For certain life policies it comes from IA GL29; general cover follows each policy's own terms.
The assessment of a customer's needs and finances that an intermediary carries out before recommending a policy, as set out in IA GL30.
A loan used to pay insurance premiums, usually for a life policy. Its standards are set by IA and HKMA circulars.

A prescribed amount the policy holder owes to the Insurance Authority and pays to the insurer with each premium for covered classes (Cap. 41 s.134(1); Cap. 41I s.3(1)). The insurer remits it to the Authority (Cap. 41I s.4).
Offering goods, services or facilities to a person, or advertising them, by sending information or messages to that person, as defined for PDPO Part 6A.
A life insurance product whose value depends on underlying investments. It is offered to the public only after authorization by the SFC under SFO s.104.

The best interests, needs analysis and disclosure duties behind every sales step are covered in depth there.
Savings, investment-linked and participating products carry extra rules before and after sale.

intro: This kit answers one question: how does a digital bank put insurance products on its app shelf and sell them to customers? It covers product due diligence, the sales journey for each product type, disclosures and documents, special customers, payments and premium financing, marketing, and after-sale servicing and complaints.

A digital bank is an authorized institution under the Banking Ordinance (Cap. 155). That status does not let it sell insurance by itself. Inviting or inducing a purchase, and advising on one, are regulated activities under Cap. 41 Sch. 1A and s.64G. The IA has delegated its inspection and investigation powers over authorized institutions' insurance business to the Monetary Authority, a delegation in place since 23 September 2019 (s.4G; reported in IA and HKMA releases), and the IA can still act itself (s.4G(5)). The IA must consult the Monetary Authority before investigating or disciplining a bank (ss.64ZZH(2), 82(4), 84(4)). The bank needs an insurance agency licence (to act for appointed insurers under s.64G(3)(a)) or an insurance broker company licence (s.64ZA). Which one depends on the model, and each needs its own conditions. The bank as an authorized institution has no general exemption for these activities. The bank also needs staff who carry on regulated activities for it to hold the right individual licence. Staff acting for a licensed insurance agency need a technical representative (agent) licence (s.64G(3)(c)).

Each activity card in this stage gives the route, the requirements, the gates Legal must clear and what to watch. Read the route line first, then the sources. Statute sections link to the official text, and other sources show their legal force, such as statutory guideline, industry code or regulator guidance.

The kit does not cover the wording of individual policies, insurer-side product approval, or the tax rules for schemes such as the Voluntary Health Insurance Scheme and QDAP. Those sit in other stages or need separate tax advice.

triage.caption: The order a digital bank should work in, from shelf selection to after-sale service.

items.label: Choose the product shelf and the insurers
items.note: Check each product's class under Cap. 41 Sch. 1 and confirm the insurer is authorized. Plan partners within the agency limits in Cap. 41K s.3.

items.label: Run product due diligence and sign-off
items.note: Test each product's cover, charges, cooling-off terms and fit with customer needs before listing. Investment-linked plans also need SFC approval. SFO s.104 (collective investment schemes) is the provision to check against the current ILAS Code (reported practice; check the current text).

items.label: Build the sales journey for each product type
items.note: Each product type needs its own journey: a needs analysis for advice, a simpler quote-and-buy path for basic cover, and a full suitability check for investment-linked plans. The core duties come from Cap. 41 s.90 and the codes issued under s.95.

items.label: Set disclosure and document rules
items.note: The customer must receive the information needed for each material decision (s.90(e)). Show key terms before the customer commits, and keep proof of delivery for the policy documents and the cooling-off notice.

items.label: Handle special customers before the journey starts
items.note: Identify elderly, vulnerable, non-Chinese-speaking and cross-border customers early, and give them extra checks and clearer language. The duty to act in the customer's best interests (s.90(a)) applies to all of them.

items.label: Settle payments, premium financing and the levy
items.note: The policy holder owes the levy to the IA (Cap. 41 s.134(1)) and pays it to the insurer with each premium (Cap. 41I s.3(1)); the insurer remits it to the IA (Cap. 41I s.4). Premium financing by a bank carries separate HKMA circular conditions (reported; check).

items.label: Clear marketing and promotions with Legal
items.note: A banner, comparison table or push message can be an invitation to buy, which is a regulated activity under s.64G and Sch. 1A. Gifts and rebates are limited by IA guideline GL25.

items.label: Set after-sale servicing and complaint routes
items.note: Tell customers how to reach the insurer and the bank. Regulatory complaints about the bank's conduct go to the HKMA; money claims go to the Financial Dispute Resolution Centre (sales) or the Insurance Complaints Bureau (policy terms and claims) (reported). Where the bank acts as a broker company, client monies must be kept separate under s.71.

items.label: Post-sale: cooling-off, renewals, claims help and complaints
items.note: Honour the cooling-off right under IA guideline GL29 for the life policies it covers (para 4.2; check the current text), and each policy's own cancellation terms for general cover.

workplan.heading: Product shelf and due diligence
workplan.lede: Only list products the bank can lawfully sell, from insurers that can lawfully sell them.
points: **Class check:** Confirm each product falls within a class in Cap. 41 Sch. 1. Para 3A bars combining long-term classes G or H with other business, unless a gazette notice under para 3B disapplies it. Para 3 treats class 1 or 2 business written in the same contract as long-term business, where the insurer is authorized for long-term business, as long-term business.

**Insurer status:** Confirm each insurer is authorized and that the bank holds an appointment for that product line. A single insurer is liable for its agent's acts in dealings with customers (s.68(2)). With several insurers, s.68(3) to (4B) decide which insurers are liable, including jointly and severally under (4A) and (4B).
**Agreement terms:** Review each partner agreement. A term that cuts across the agent's duty to customers under s.90(a) is void (s.68A).
**Product approval:** Record a product committee decision for each product. The record should cover the class, charges, cooling-off terms, target customers and fit with the bank's customer base.

**Investment-linked and protection-linked plans:** These need extra approvals. Investment-linked plans also need SFC approval; SFO s.104 (collective investment schemes) is the provision to check against the current ILAS Code. Protection-linked plan sales follow HKMA circulars. HKMA circulars on selling protection linked plans (8 July 2022 and 30 August 2023) are reported to expect a bank to discuss an ILAS launch with the HKMA beforehand (reported; check both circulars).

workplan.heading: Sales journeys and conduct
workplan.lede: Every journey must meet the conduct duties in s.90 before a customer can buy.
points: **Core duties:** A licensed intermediary must act honestly, fairly and in the best interests of the policy holder. It must also use care, skill and diligence, as set out in s.90(a) and (b).
**Needs analysis:** IA guideline GL30 requires a financial needs analysis before a policy is recommended. Check the current text before fixing the questions in the journey.

**Conflicts:** The intermediary must use its best endeavours to avoid conflicts between its interests and the customer's, and must disclose any conflict it cannot avoid (s.90(f) and (g)). Bank incentives tied to a policy need this review.
**Advice boundary:** An intermediary may advise only on matters it is competent to advise on (s.90(c)). Scripts, chat and help content must stay within the licence scope.

**Remote and video sales:** HKMA circulars allow risk-based alternatives to audio recording for some sales (reported, December 2024). Confirm the IA position on video sales of long-term products before launch (reported; check).

workplan.heading: Disclosures and documents
workplan.lede: Disclosure is a legal duty, and the bank must be able to prove that it was made.
points: **Material information:** The intermediary must disclose what the customer needs to be sufficiently informed for each material decision (s.90(e)). Sch. 1A defines the material decisions.
**Records of advice:** Keep records of the needs analysis, the recommendation and the customer's answers. Inspectors may require these records (s.64ZZF).

**Cooling-off notice:** IA guideline GL29 gives a cooling-off period, with a premium refund, of 21 calendar days for certain types of life insurance policies (its para 4.2 lists them; check the current text). It is a guideline under s.133, not law in itself. For general cover, check each policy's own cancellation terms.
**Language:** Provide key documents in the language the customer uses, and check that the app and the policy documents match. This is good practice, not a statutory test.
**Point-of-sale disclosure:** Show the key terms before the customer commits, not only in a follow-up email. This is good practice and supports the disclosure duty in s.90(e).

workplan.heading: Special customers
workplan.lede: Some customers need extra checks, and a fully online journey can miss them.
points: **Vulnerable customers:** Elderly customers, people with limited financial knowledge and people under financial stress need slower journeys and extra checks. This is good practice, reflecting the duty to act in the customer's best interests (s.90(a)).
**Buying for others:** A parent buying for a child, or a relative buying for another person, needs the right policy holder and insured person. Check who signs, who pays and who receives the benefit.

**Cross-border customers:** A person who actively markets insurance services to the public from outside Hong Kong is treated as holding out that it carries on a regulated activity, which s.64G(2) prohibits (s.64H(1)). Group entities and partners marketing from overseas need the same review.
**Non-Chinese speakers:** Offer the key information in the language the customer reads, and test the journey in that language. This is good practice.
**Business buyers:** A business buying cover is a different customer type. Check whether the product class, the disclosure duties and the cooling-off terms change for that customer.

workplan.heading: Payments, premium financing and the levy
workplan.lede: Money moves at several points in the sale, and each point carries a legal duty.
points: **Levy liability:** The policy holder owes the levy to the IA (Cap. 41 s.134(1)) and pays it to the insurer with each premium (Cap. 41I s.3(1)); the insurer remits it to the IA (Cap. 41I s.4).

**Levy amount:** From 1 April 2021 the levy is 0.1% of each premium, capped at HK$5,000 for specified general business and HK$100 for specified long term business per policy year (Cap. 41J, ss.5 and 6 and the Schedule).

**Levy handling:** An intermediary that collects levy money must pass it to the insurer as soon as practicable, and the insurer may not keep any excess (Cap. 41I s.3(2) and (3)). A policy holder who does not pay the levy can face a penalty of up to HK$5,000 (s.3(4)).

**Premium financing:** A bank that acts as both the intermediary and the premium financier must keep the lending and the insurance sale separate. HKMA circulars from 2022 onward set the conditions (reported; check the current version).
**Payment channels:** Premium payments made in the app must match the policy's payment terms and reach the insurer on time. Test the refund and failed-payment paths as well as the happy path.

workplan.heading: Marketing and promotions
workplan.lede: Marketing in the app is part of the sale, so it carries the same legal risk.
points: **Invitation to buy:** Banners, comparison tables and push messages can invite or induce a purchase, which is a regulated activity under s.64G and Sch. 1A. Legal should review each campaign before it runs.

**Gifts and rebates:** IA guideline GL25 bars gifts for Class C products, and allows more flexibility for other classes (check the current text). Premium rebates on long-term products are allowed only if they meet GL25's criteria.
**Return-enhancing promotions:** A HKMA circular of 19 November 2025 is reported to stress separating financing from insurance applications and to bar return-enhancing promotions (reported; check).
**Referral fees:** The IA issued a circular on 1 September 2025 on referral fees paid by broker companies for participating policies (reported; check the text and any benchmark).
**Direct marketing:** Using customer data to market insurance must follow the PDPO (Cap. 486), including the consent and opt-out rules for direct marketing.

workplan.heading: After-sale servicing and complaints
workplan.lede: The sale does not end at payment. Customers need help with changes, claims and disputes.
points: **Cooling-off and cancellation:** Process cancellations within the cooling-off period and refund the premium promptly. Test this path before launch, not only the purchase path.
**Renewals and changes:** Track renewal dates, premium changes and policy changes, and send notices in time for the customer to act.
**Claims help:** The insurer decides claims. The bank's role is to route the customer and explain the process, not to decide or promise payment. Keep that line clear in scripts and in the app.

**Complaints route:** Two tracks. A regulatory complaint about the bank's conduct as an agency goes to the HKMA, which handles complaints about authorized institutions' insurance business under the 2019 IA-HKMA memorandum (reported). A money claim goes to the Financial Dispute Resolution Centre if it is about how the bank sold the product (reported from bank disclosures), or to the Insurance Complaints Bureau if it is a personal policy-term or claims dispute with the insurer (reported; check its current scope and limit).

**Review and compensation:** The Insurance Appeals Tribunal under Cap. 41 Part XII hears applications for review of specified decisions. A Policyholders' Protection Scheme was consulted on in 2022 and 2023, but no official timetable has been confirmed (proposal; reported).

activities.title: Travel, home and other general insurance
activities.summary: The bank sells short-term general cover such as travel and home policies. Each product falls in a general class in Schedule 1, and the bank's licence must cover every class it sells. The full set of intermediary conduct duties applies, including the duty to disclose conflicts.
activities.route: Yes, but only through a licence. The bank needs a licensed insurance agency or broker company licence under Cap. 41 s.64G, and the licence must list each general line the bank sells. A new line needs an approved variation under s.64S before launch.
require: **Licence scope:** The licence must cover each general class the bank sells, such as class 1 accident, class 8 fire and natural forces, class 9 damage to property and class 17 legal expenses (Sch. 1 Pt 3, s.64U(4)).

**Technical representatives:** A staff member who gives regulated advice needs a technical representative licence, and an agency representative may act only in a line the agency is licensed for (s.64L(2)).

**Appointment model:** An agency acts for an authorized insurer that appoints it, while a broker company acts as agent of the policy holder (s.64G(3)(a) and (d)). The model must be settled before the licence application.

**Insurer referrals:** An authorized insurer may accept business only through a licensed intermediary or a clerical role, so the insurer cannot take the bank's referrals unless the bank is licensed (s.64N(1)-(2)).

**Levy:** The policy holder owes the levy to the IA (Cap. 41 s.134(1)) and pays it to the insurer with each premium (Cap. 41I s.3(1)); the insurer remits it to the IA (Cap. 41I s.4). An intermediary that collects it must forward it to the insurer as soon as practicable (Cap. 41I s.3(2)). The levy covers specified general or long term business, excluding reinsurance and captive contracts, in general classes 1, 2, 3, 4, 8, 9, 10, 13, 14, 15, 16 and 17 (Cap. 41J s.2 and s.4).

**Code of conduct:** The IA code of conduct for agents is issued under s.95, and a broker code applies to broker companies (reported). A breach does not by itself create liability, but it can count against the bank's fitness to remain licensed (s.95(5)-(6)).

**Licence application:** The agency licence application must be accompanied either by a technical representative application and a responsible officer application, or by a responsible officer application for a licensed technical representative (s.64U(3)). The applicant must also be appointed by at least one authorized insurer (s.64U(5)(b)).
gates: **Licence scope check:** Confirm in writing that every general product falls in a class the licence covers, before the product goes live.
**Product mapping:** Map each product to a Schedule 1 class and record the reason, product by product, since an app bundle can mix classes.
**Disclosure and conflicts:** Build the disclosure of the bank's interest and any conflict (s.90(e)-(g)) into the app before a quote is shown.
**Needs check:** Confirm the journey asks about the customer's circumstances that matter for the cover, and records the answers (s.90(d)).

**Cooling-off:** IA guideline GL29 gives a cooling-off period of 21 calendar days for certain types of life insurance policies (its para 4.2 lists them; check the current text). For general cover, check each policy's own cancellation terms before build.
**Levy and premium display:** Confirm the levy amount and how it is remitted to the IA through the insurer, before any premium is displayed.
watchFor: **Selling outside the licence:** A licence covers only the lines listed in it (s.64G(1), s.64U(4)). Adding a new cover line to the app without an approved variation is an offence risk.
**Agent exposure:** If the app quotes, binds and takes premiums for an insurer, the insurer is answerable for the acts of its appointed agent (s.68). Check the appointment wording before launch.
**Referral partners:** A partner that refers customers into the app must be a licensed intermediary or fall within the clerical exception, or the insurer cannot accept the referral (s.64N(2)).

activities.title: Term life, critical illness and accident cover
activities.summary: The bank sells term life, critical illness and accident cover. Death and lump-sum benefits sit in long term class A, income cover for long-term incapacity sits in class D, and accident-only benefits can sit in general class 1. Needs analysis, cooling-off, underwriting and health data are the main legal points.
activities.route: Yes, through a licensed insurance agency appointed by the insurer, with each long term class named on the licence (Cap. 41 s.64G and s.64U(4)). Staff who advise need technical representative licences, and the bank must not sell a benefit in a class its licence does not cover.
require: **Classification:** Check each benefit against Schedule 1. Sums payable on death are class A life. Incapacity cover is class D only if it runs for at least 5 years, to retirement age or without limit, and the insurer can terminate it only in special circumstances stated in the contract. Accident-only benefits can be class 1.
**Licence scope:** The agency licence must list every long term and general class sold (s.64U(4)). Adding a line needs an approved variation (s.64S).
**Financial needs analysis:** An intermediary must carry out a financial needs analysis before recommending a policy, under IA guideline GL30 (reported; check the current text).

**Cooling-off:** IA guideline GL29 gives a cooling-off period of 21 calendar days for certain types of life insurance policies (its para 4.2 lists them; check the current text). It is a guideline under s.133, not law in itself. The period is reported to run from delivery of the policy or a cooling-off notice, whichever is earlier. The app must support a cancel and refund within that period.

**Underwriting guideline:** The IA is reported to have revised GL16 (underwriting long term business other than class C) on 6 February 2026, effective 31 March 2026 (reported; check the IA text). Ask the insurer whether the revision changes the health questions, and record its answer.
**Health data:** Health answers are personal data under the Personal Data (Privacy) Ordinance (Cap. 486). Limit collection to what underwriting needs and tell the customer how the data will be used.
gates: **Licence and class check:** Confirm the licence covers each long term and general class for every benefit before the product goes live.
**Needs analysis in the journey:** Build the financial needs analysis into the app before any recommendation, and keep the record that supports it (GL30).
**Cooling-off test:** Test the cancellation flow end to end, including the refund and the timing of the cooling-off notice.
**Underwriting sign-off:** Get the insurer to approve the health questions against its own underwriting rules. The insurer, not the bank, decides acceptance.
**Data protection review:** Complete a privacy review of the health data flow and agree with the insurer who holds the data and for how long (Cap. 486).
**Benefit illustrations:** Where the app shows any benefit figure, follow the illustration rules in GL28 before publication.
**Disclosure review:** Check app copy and product summaries against the disclosure duty for material decisions (s.90(e)).
watchFor: **Fast quote without underwriting:** A quick quote that skips health questions can suggest cover the insurer will not give. Show the conditions for acceptance beside the quote.
**Mislabelled accident cover:** Accident cover can be general class 1 or part of a long term class D contract. The app label should match the classification in Schedule 1.
**Late cancellation costs:** After the cooling-off period, cancelling can cost the customer money. Show that cost before the customer acts (s.90(e)).

activities.title: Medical insurance and VHIS plans
activities.summary: The bank sells medical insurance, including plans certified under the Voluntary Health Insurance Scheme (VHIS). Whether the cover is long term or general decides which licence and duties apply. Renewals are material decisions, and certification is a Health Bureau matter, not an IA one.
activities.route: Yes, through the same licensed agency or broker route as other health cover (Cap. 41 s.64G). VHIS certification is a Health Bureau matter, so the bank should check each plan's certification at launch and at each renewal before it offers the plan for the tax deduction.
require: **Classification:** Long term class D covers permanent health cover that runs for at least 5 years, to retirement age or without limit, and that the insurer can terminate only in special circumstances stated in the contract. Shorter or annual sickness cover is general class 2.

**Renewal is a material decision:** Issuance, continuance and renewal of a contract are matters specified for regulated activity (Sch. 1A Pt 2 para 1(b)). Advice or an offer made at renewal therefore needs a licensed intermediary and carries the disclosure duties.

**VHIS certification:** Certified plans are individual indemnity hospital plans certified by the Health Bureau. Only the premium for the certified plan counts toward the tax deduction (reported; check the official page).
**Tax deduction:** The cap and the year-of-assessment wording should be checked against the official tax page on the day of launch. The app must not describe a whole bundled premium as deductible.
**Plan terms:** Check whether the Health Bureau sets standard terms for certified plans. If it does, show those terms in the app's product features (reported; check the current text).
**Health data:** Medical questions and claims data are personal data under Cap. 486. Limit what the app collects and keep claims data within the insurer's processes.
gates: **Certification check:** Confirm each plan is certified and still on the Health Bureau list at launch and at every renewal.
**Classification sign-off:** Get written sign-off from the insurer and Legal on whether each medical product is class D or class 2.
**Renewal journey:** Show any change in terms or premium before renewal takes effect, and record the disclosure as a material decision (Sch. 1A Pt 2).
**Tax wording approval:** Approve the deduction wording and the cap with Tax and Legal before it goes live.
**Advice boundary:** Decide whether the app gives information only or regulated advice at renewal (Sch. 1A Pt 1 para 1(d)). If it gives advice, the staff and licence must cover it.
**Data flows:** Agree with the insurer who holds medical and claims data and how it is kept (Cap. 486).
watchFor: **Bundled premiums:** A policy that combines a certified plan with other cover needs the split shown clearly. Customers may assume the whole premium is deductible.
**Renewal changes:** A renewal that changes terms or premiums is a material decision, so the change must be disclosed before it takes effect.
**Mislabelled medical cover:** Presenting a short annual sickness policy as long term may suggest class D protections it does not have.

activities.title: Savings and participating policies
activities.summary: The bank sells savings and participating life policies, where the return depends on the insurer's bonuses and experience. Benefit illustrations are the main legal risk, along with replacement, surrender losses and bank selling standards.
activities.route: Yes, through a licensed insurance agency appointed by the insurer that issues the policy (Cap. 41 s.64G and s.64U). The non-linked savings line sits in long term class A, and the IA has delegated its inspection and investigation powers over authorized institutions' insurance business to the Monetary Authority, a delegation in place since 23 September 2019 (s.4G; reported in IA and HKMA releases), and the IA can still act itself (s.4G(5)).
require: **Classification:** Non-linked savings and participating policies sit in long term class A (life and annuity). Linked savings fall in class C and are covered on the ILAS card.
**Benefit illustrations:** Illustrations must follow GL28. The IA practice note of 28 February 2025 sets rate caps for illustrations of participating policies (reported; check the note).
**Needs analysis:** An intermediary must carry out a financial needs analysis before recommending a savings policy, under GL30 (reported; check).
**Policy replacement:** Replacing one long term policy with another is covered by IA guideline GL27. Interpretation notes issued on 22 September 2020 cover GL25 and GL27 (reported).
**Surrender losses:** The bank must disclose the cost of early surrender and of stopping premiums before the customer commits (s.90(e); Sch. 1A Pt 2 para 1(c)).
**Bank selling standards:** The HKMA's 2014 letter on selling non-linked long-term insurance, and its 2020 review of bank selling practices, set the expectations for bank sales (reported; check).
gates: **Illustration controls:** Confirm the illustration tool applies the rate caps and the GL28 format before any figure appears in the app.
**Replacement check:** Build a prompt that compares the old and new policy before a switch is confirmed, and keep the record of it.
**Surrender warning:** Show the surrender value and the loss on early exit at the point of sale, not only in the policy terms.
**Non-guaranteed elements:** Say in plain words that bonuses and other non-guaranteed amounts can change, next to any illustrated figure.
**Needs record:** Keep the needs analysis answers and the reasons for the recommended product, for the period Legal confirms.
**Commission and conflicts:** Disclose the bank's commission and any conflict under s.90(e)-(g) before the sale.
**HKMA engagement (good practice):** Discuss the shelf, target customers and sales channel with the HKMA before launch, and keep a note of its feedback.
watchFor: **Illustrations read as forecasts:** Illustrated returns can look like promises. Never show a best-case figure on its own.
**Churning:** Prompts or staff incentives that encourage switching between policies can breach the replacement rules (GL27).
**Deposit comparisons:** Comparing a savings policy with a bank deposit can mislead on liquidity and on what is guaranteed.

activities.title: Annuities and qualifying deferred annuities
activities.summary: The bank sells annuities, including qualifying deferred annuity policies (QDAPs) that the IA certifies for a tax deduction. A deferred annuity on a human life is long term class A. Certification, the limits of the tax claim and the split between guaranteed and non-guaranteed benefits must be clear in the app.
activities.route: Yes, through a licensed agency or broker route (Cap. 41 s.64G) for an insurer's deferred annuity. Only premiums for IA-certified QDAPs qualify for the deduction, so the bank may describe the tax benefit only for a certified product and must check the current certified list before launch.
require: **Classification:** A deferred annuity on a human life is long term class A (life and annuity). A linked annuity falls in class C, which carries the ILAS rules.
**QDAP certification:** Only premiums for IA-certified QDAPs qualify for the deduction, and the IA publishes the certified list (reported; check the current list).

**Deduction cap:** The IA page is reported to set a cap of HK$60,000 a year of assessment, shared with MPF voluntary contributions. Confirm the figure on the IA page before showing it to any customer (reported).

**Eligibility caveat:** Issuer material says certification does not guarantee the deduction, which depends on the taxpayer's own position (reported). Avoid promising tax relief, and have Tax confirm the wording.
**Guaranteed and non-guaranteed benefits:** Show guaranteed amounts separately from non-guaranteed ones, and follow GL28 for any illustration.

**Video-conference sales:** The HKMA's December 2024 circular is reported to cover video-conference sales of investment products, with recording or alternative digital controls. Whether it also reaches annuity sales is a point to check in the HKMA text (reported).
gates: **Certification gate:** Confirm the product is on the IA's certified QDAP list on launch day and check again at each renewal.
**Tax claim approval:** Approve every tax statement, cap and eligibility wording with Legal and Tax before it goes live.
**Product criteria check:** Use the IA guideline criteria, not an issuer's example, for any minimum premium, payment term or annuitisation age.
**Needs analysis:** Carry out a financial needs analysis under GL30 before a deferred annuity is recommended, and record the customer's age and income position.
**Video-sale controls:** For any video-conference sale, apply the HKMA's recording or alternative measures and keep the record (reported).
**Surrender cost:** Show the cost of early surrender, and any effect on the tax position, at the point of sale.

**Complaints route:** A regulatory complaint about the bank's conduct as an agency goes to the HKMA (reported). A money claim about how the bank sold the product goes to the Financial Dispute Resolution Centre (reported from bank disclosures). A personal policy-term or claims dispute with the insurer goes to the Insurance Complaints Bureau (reported).
watchFor: **Tax promises:** Telling customers they will get the deduction can mislead them, because it depends on their own tax position.
**Certification lapses:** A product that loses certification, or changes in a way that affects it, can lose its tax status. The app must reflect the current status.
**Shortcuts in video sales:** Skipping the identity or recording steps to speed onboarding can breach the HKMA's expectations for remote sales.

activities.title: Investment-linked assurance schemes
activities.summary: The bank sells investment-linked assurance schemes (ILAS), life policies whose value depends on underlying investments. They are long term class C business under Cap. 41, and the SFC authorizes the scheme and any public offering document under the SFO. The sale needs insurance, securities and banking controls at once.
activities.route: Yes, as a licensed intermediary for an insurer's ILAS, but only once the SFC has authorized the scheme under SFO s.104 and any public offering document under s.105. Whether the bank needs its own SFC licence to distribute ILAS is for the SFC to say, so get a written SFC view before launch.
require: **Class C:** ILAS are linked long term business under class C of Schedule 1 Pt 2, where benefits depend on the value of or income from property. Class C products are subject to the IA rules for linked business and the SFO authorization route.

**SFC authorization:** The SFC may authorize a collective investment scheme under SFO s.104, subject to conditions including an approved person for SFC notices. A public offering document needs its own authorization under s.105.

**Unauthorized public offer:** Under SFO s.103, issuing an advertisement or document that invites the public to buy an interest in a scheme without authorization is an offence. The carve-out for offers disposed of only to professional investors is in s.103(2)(k), so a retail ILAS offer is not covered by it.

**Dealing licence question:** The SFO Sch. 5 exemption covers transactions by an authorized insurer for its insurance business. It does not name intermediaries, so the bank's position is not settled by that exemption. The SFC view is needed.

**Securities definition:** SFO Sch. 1, Pt 1 excludes from 'securities' an interest in a collective investment scheme that is a contract of insurance in a Cap. 41 Sch. 1 class. On that reading an insurance-wrapped ILAS may sit outside 'dealing in securities', but that is not a settled SFC position, so get the SFC's written view before launch.

**Suitability tools:** HKMA guidance on protection-linked plans points to the financial needs analysis and risk profile questionnaire in IA guidelines GL26 and GL30 (reported; check the titles and the current texts).
**No gifts:** For class C business, insurers and intermediaries may not offer gifts when marketing or distributing it (GL25, reported).
gates: **SFC authorization check:** Confirm that the scheme and each offering document are authorized under s.104 and s.105 before the app shows them.
**Dealing licence view:** Get the SFC's written view on whether the bank needs a licence for ILAS distribution before the product committee approves launch.

**HKMA prior notice:** HKMA circulars on selling protection linked plans (8 July 2022 and 30 August 2023) are reported to expect a bank to discuss an ILAS launch with the HKMA beforehand (reported; check both circulars).

**Suitability journey:** Build the risk profile questionnaire and the needs analysis into the app. Check whether the HKMA audio-recording rule for complex products covers face-to-face ILAS sales, and apply the ILAS segregation measures (25 September 2019 circular, reported).
**Benefit disclosure:** Disclose the bank's monetary and non-monetary benefits in writing before sale, as the HKMA's 2013 circular required (reported).
**Gifts and rewards:** Remove any gift or reward from the ILAS campaign, including referral incentives.
**Advertising review:** Review ILAS advertising against the SFO s.103 rules and the SFC's requirements before publication.
watchFor: **Mislabelled as a deposit or fund:** Customers must see that it is investment-linked insurance with investment risk. The HKMA's 2011 measures required clear upfront identification (reported).
**Charges not understood:** Customers may not follow the charges and surrender costs. Show them in the app before the customer commits.
**Marketing like a fund:** Advertising an ILAS as if it were a unit trust can breach the offer rules in s.103 and s.105 if no authorization covers it.

activities.title: Premium financing for life policies
activities.summary: Premium financing is a loan that pays life policy premiums, often arranged by the bank that also sells the policy. Because the bank is both lender and agency, conflicts and interest-rate terms are the main legal issues. The IA and HKMA have set standards for this activity.
activities.route: Yes, if the bank holds the insurance agency licence and lends under its banking licence. Its dual role triggers the conflict duties in Cap. 41 s.90(f)-(g), and the IA and HKMA premium financing standards apply from 1 January 2023 (reported; check).
require: **Dual role:** The bank is both lender and insurance agency for the same policy. Section 90(f) requires the bank to use its best endeavours to avoid a conflict with the customer's interests, and s.90(g) requires disclosure of any such conflict.
**Standards:** IA and HKMA circulars on premium financing of 1 April 2022 apply from 1 January 2023 (reported; check the current texts).

**Separation:** The HKMA's review findings of 19 November 2025 are reported to call for separating financing from the insurance application, and for banning return-enhancing promotions (reported; check).
**Interest-rate basis:** Loan clauses that change the interest-rate basis for premium financing are the subject of the HKMA's 16 October 2023 circular (reported; check).

**Steering:** The IA's 2019 explanatory note for banks is reported to treat referrals made with preferential financing rates as regulated activity. Check whether the loan offer invites the customer to buy a policy (Sch. 1A Pt 1 para 1(b)-(c)) and whether s.64N is engaged (reported; check).
**Concentration:** An IA circular dated 20 August 2026 is reported to address concentrated premium-financing exposures for long-term policies (reported; check).
gates: **Separated journeys:** Run the loan application as its own journey, with its own consent and disclosure, separate from the policy application.
**No return-enhancing promotions:** Remove any offer that promises a higher policy return from financing, and check the marketing copy against the HKMA's findings.
**Conflict assessment:** Document the s.90(f) conflict assessment and the s.90(g) disclosure before the product goes live.
**Rate basis clauses:** Check each loan agreement's interest-rate clause against the HKMA's 16 October 2023 circular.
**Collateral and credit review:** Assess the policy as collateral, the lending limits, and the risk that the policy's value does not cover the loan.
**Incentives:** Remove sales incentives that tie lending to policy sales or steer customers toward financing.
**Board approval:** Get risk committee approval of the exposure limits, in light of the IA's 2026 circular on concentrated exposures.
watchFor: **Loan as a sales hook:** A financing offer in the policy journey can push customers into a policy they do not need. Keep the policy choice separate.
**Rising interest rates:** A rate rise can make a financed premium unaffordable and leave the customer with a loan the policy does not cover.
**Stale standards:** The IA circular dated 20 August 2026 and the HKMA's November 2025 findings may change the standards. Check the current texts before launch.

activities.title: Buying in the app without advice
activities.summary: The customer buys a policy in the bank's app without speaking to an adviser. The sale is still a regulated activity, because negotiating, arranging, inviting and inducing a contract of insurance are caught by Schedule 1A, so the bank needs its own licence and the conduct duties in s.90 still apply.
activities.route: Yes, through the bank's own licensed insurance agency or broker company, with each product covered by the licences of the technical representatives behind the journey. Before launching an ILAS or protection linked plan, discuss it with the HKMA: HKMA circulars on selling protection linked plans (8 July 2022 and 30 August 2023) are reported to expect a bank to discuss an ILAS launch with the HKMA beforehand (reported; check both circulars). Keep the journey execution-only in fact, because a recommendation turns it into regulated advice.
require: **Licence first:** s.64G(1) bars a person from carrying on a regulated activity in the course of business or for reward. Schedule 1A Part 1 lists negotiating, arranging, inviting and inducing as regulated activities, so the bank needs a licence even when it gives no advice.

**No-advice label:** A label such as 'no advice needed' does not take a sale outside the rules. A button, prompt or quote that invites a customer to buy is an invitation under Schedule 1A Part 1, item 1(b).

**Conduct duties:** s.90 applies to every regulated activity. The bank must act honestly and fairly (s.90(a)), must have regard to the customer's circumstances so the sale is appropriate (s.90(d)), and must disclose what the customer needs to make an informed decision (s.90(e)).

**Execution-only status:** Whether IA Guideline GL30, the financial needs analysis, applies to execution-only long term sales is unsettled (reported; check). Until Legal answers it, treat the point as open rather than settled.

**E-signature:** Cap. 553 s.6(1) lets an electronic signature satisfy a signature requirement if the method is reliable and appropriate for the purpose and the other party consents. s.17(2A) stops an electronic signature losing legal effect only because it is electronic. The insurer's own signing rules still apply.

**Cooling-off:** IA guideline GL29 gives a cooling-off period of 21 calendar days for certain types of life insurance policies (its para 4.2 lists them; check the current text). For general cover, check each policy's own cancellation terms. It is a guideline under Cap. 41 s.133, not law in itself: a breach does not by itself create liability, but a court takes its relevant provisions into account (s.133). Show the cancellation right and the refund route in the app.

**Journey testing and records:** Test each screen path before launch, including warnings and error states, and keep dated versions of the journey and its disclosures. Treat this as good practice; check whether the IA sets specific record rules for execution-only sales.
gates: **Licence coverage:** Confirm that the bank's agency or broker licence, and its technical representatives' licences, cover every product and every app screen that invites a purchase. Get the answer in writing before the product committee meets.
**Advice boundary:** Review sales copy, comparison tables, rankings, FAQs and push messages. Any opinion on a Schedule 1A Part 3 matter is regulated advice under s.3A(c).
**GL30 position:** Get Legal's written view on whether GL30 applies to execution-only long term sales. Record the answer and the reasons, since it decides whether the app needs a needs-analysis step.

**Disclosure before payment:** Confirm that the product's disclosure documents and the cooling-off notice appear in the app before the customer pays, so the s.90(e) duty is met at the point of decision.

**Electronic signature consent:** Record the customer's consent to e-signature under Cap. 553 s.6(1)(e), and confirm with each insurer that its application and policy forms accept electronic signatures.

**Marketing consent split:** Keep purchase data separate from marketing consent. Direct marketing needs consent under PDPO s.35E, and a breach is an offence with a fine of HK$500,000 and 3 years' imprisonment on conviction.
**Release sign-off:** Compliance signs off the test record for each journey release, including the cooling-off and cancellation route.
watchFor: **No-advice claims:** Copy saying the bank 'does not advise' does not change the licence position, and it can mislead the customer under s.90(a). Compliance should check the wording.

**Drift into advice:** Ranking, 'best for you' tags and quiz-based suggestions can turn an execution-only journey into regulated advice. s.123(1)(f) exempts advice given through electronic communication to the public, but it does not cover arranging or inviting a sale, and it is no safe harbour for a personal recommendation.
**Open GL30 point:** Do not assume GL30 is switched off for execution-only sales. The point stays open until Legal answers it.

activities.title: Advice by video, chat or a relationship manager
activities.summary: The customer gets advice from an adviser, a relationship manager or a chatbot without meeting in person, by video, chat or phone. Advice on a Schedule 1A Part 3 matter is regulated advice, so every adviser must be licensed and competent. Remote channels change how the advice is evidenced, not whether it is regulated.
activities.route: Yes, if every adviser is a licensed technical representative of the bank's agency or broker company and advises only within competence (s.90(c)). Remote delivery also needs the HKMA's non-face-to-face and recording measures, and the status of the IA's video-conference measures must be confirmed before launch.
require: **Licensed advisers only:** Only the bank's licensed agency or broker company, acting through licensed individual agents or technical representatives, may give regulated advice for the bank (s.64G(1), with the exceptions in s.64G(3)). A relationship manager who discusses policy terms without a licence breaches s.64G(1).
**Competence:** s.90(c) limits advice to matters the intermediary is competent to advise on. Set a product-by-product competence list for each adviser, and enforce it in the tools they use.

**Needs analysis:** IA Guideline GL30 requires a financial needs analysis before a policy is recommended (reported; check the current text). s.90(d) separately requires regard to the customer's circumstances, so build the needs step into the remote flow before any recommendation.

**Remote-sale measures:** The HKMA circular of 24 September 2021 covers distribution of investment and insurance products through non-face-to-face channels, including video conference (reported; check). The IA's circular of 5 August 2020 set conditions for video-conference sales of long term policies, but check whether it is still in force.

**Recording and identity:** The HKMA circular of December 2024 allows alternatives to audio recording for video-conference sales of investment and annuity products, provided controls such as identity authentication and secure video facilities apply (reported; check). Keep a record of each session in a form the bank can produce.

**Disclosure and conflicts:** s.90(e) requires disclosure enough for an informed decision. s.90(f) and (g) require the bank to avoid conflicts where it can and to disclose any that remain, which covers relationship manager targets and incentives.

**Records of advice:** Keep a record of the needs analysis, the advice given and the customer's acceptance, whichever channel was used. Treat this as good practice; check whether the IA sets specific record rules for remote advice.
gates: **Adviser licence check:** Before first contact, confirm each adviser's licence status on the IA register and the bank's agency or broker licence. Block any adviser whose licence does not cover the product.
**Competence matrix:** Approve the product list for each adviser, and block product information outside it in the chat and video tools.
**Regulator position:** Confirm with the IA and HKMA the current status of the video-conference measures and of the December 2024 circular before design freeze.
**Identity and session controls:** Test identity checks, the secure video set-up, and the alternative confirmation step that applies when the adviser doubts the customer.

**Chatbot classification:** Classify every chatbot answer as general information, a sales invitation or regulated advice. Route regulated advice to a licensed adviser, and check the wording against Schedule 1A Part 3.
**Incentive review:** Review relationship manager pay, targets and product bonuses against s.90(f) and (g) before launch, and set disclosure wording for any conflict that remains.
**Needs step sign-off:** Compliance signs off the GL30 needs step and the record it produces before any remote recommendation goes live.
watchFor: **Chatbot as adviser:** An answer such as 'this policy suits you' is regulated advice. s.123(1)(f) exempts advice through electronic communication to the public, but a one-to-one chat is unlikely to fall within it. Legal should confirm.
**Unlicensed relationship managers:** A relationship manager who discusses policy terms outside their licence breaches s.64G(1), whatever the channel.
**Gaps in evidence:** Chats or calls that are not kept can leave the bank unable to prove what advice was given, which weakens its position on suitability.

activities.title: Elderly and vulnerable customers
activities.summary: Older and vulnerable customers can be harmed most by sales of long term and investment-linked policies. Check whether any IA rule specific to elderly customers applies. Until then, the duties that bite are the general conduct duties in s.90 and the HKMA's investor-protection measures. The bank should apply those duties with extra care, and treat the extra steps below as good practice where no specific rule applies.
activities.route: Yes, the bank can sell to older and vulnerable customers under the same licence and conduct rules, plus its own vulnerability policy. Consider raising the approach with the HKMA relationship team before launch (good practice).
require: **Core conduct duties:** s.90(a) requires the bank to act honestly, fairly and in the customer's best interests. s.90(d) requires regard to the customer's circumstances, which matters more when the customer may be vulnerable.
**Disclosure:** s.90(e) requires enough information for an informed decision. Plain-language key points and a clear cooling-off route are the practical steps for older customers.

**HKMA investor protection:** The HKMA circular of 25 September 2019 covers investment, insurance and MPF sales, including audio recording for face-to-face sales of complex products (reported; check the text). Check what it says about vulnerable customers.

**Cooling-off:** IA guideline GL29 gives a cooling-off period of 21 calendar days for certain types of life insurance policies (its para 4.2 lists them; check the current text). For general cover, check each policy's own cancellation terms. Older customers need a clear reminder of whichever right applies.

**Age and change triggers:** Check whether an IA rule specific to older customers applies; an age-based flag is good practice either way. Flag customers for an extra review on age band, bereavement, a change in health or a first purchase.

**Third parties present:** Where a family member or other third party is present, the adviser or the app should confirm that the customer makes the decision. This is good practice; check whether a specific rule applies.
**Post-sale contact:** Check whether any IA or HKMA rule requires a call after the sale. A check-in call for flagged customers is good practice.
gates: **Vulnerability policy:** Compliance approves a written policy that defines vulnerable customers, lists the triggers and sets the response for each trigger.
**Flag and referral path:** The app flags triggers and routes flagged customers to a trained adviser before any purchase is completed.
**Needs review:** For flagged customers, run a needs review under GL30 (reported) before any recommendation, and confirm whether GL30 applies to the product.
**Training:** Front-line staff complete training on recognising vulnerability, with records kept. A code of conduct can require continuing training (s.95(3)(b)).
**Monitoring:** Track complaints, cancellations and early surrenders by age band and by flag, and review the results each quarter.
**Guidance check:** Legal confirms whether any IA or HKMA guidance specific to older or vulnerable customers exists; the point stays open until then.
**Sign-off:** The board or risk committee signs off the vulnerability policy and the monitoring measures.
watchFor: **Pressure selling:** Countdown timers, limited-time offers or repeated prompts aimed at older customers can breach the honesty and fairness duty in s.90(a).
**Generic checks:** A standard eligibility check does not show that a customer understands the product. Flagged customers need a human check.
**Silence is not clearance:** Where no rule specific to older customers applies, s.90 still applies in full. Do not treat the gap as permission.

activities.title: Non-resident and mainland customers
activities.summary: Many digital bank customers live or move outside Hong Kong. Selling Hong Kong policies to mainland residents, or to mainland visitors in Hong Kong, raises three separate questions: the IA's requirements for mainland policyholders, the bank's customer due diligence for non-resident customers, and whether mainland rules allow the sale at all.
activities.route: Yes for customers in Hong Kong, including mainland visitors, once the Important Facts Statement step is built. Selling to mainland residents, or using service centres in the Greater Bay Area, needs separate mainland advice and a licensing check before launch.
require: **Important Facts Statement:** A 2016 IA circular requires an Important Facts Statement for new individual long term applications from mainland visitors, and insurers must have a way to confirm that the customer understood it (reported; check the circular). The app must show the statement and capture the acknowledgement.
**Disclosure duty:** s.90(e) requires disclosure enough for an informed decision, so the Important Facts Statement step supports the statutory duty as well as the circular.

**Non-resident due diligence:** Schedule 2 to Cap. 615 sets the customer due diligence and record-keeping duties the bank must meet. Legal should check the full text for the rules that apply to non-resident customers.

**Marketing from outside Hong Kong:** s.64H treats active marketing to the public from a place outside Hong Kong as holding out. It is aimed at overseas marketers, so it does not settle where the bank's sale takes place. Legal should confirm the position for each customer group.

**Mainland law:** Whether mainland law lets mainland residents buy Hong Kong policies, or lets a Hong Kong bank sell them, is a separate question. Mainland counsel should advise before any feature for mainland residents goes live (check).

**Greater Bay Area service:** Some insurers reportedly run after-sales service centres in the Greater Bay Area for Hong Kong policyholders (reported; check the arrangements and the licensing position).

**Language and format:** Give the Important Facts Statement and product documents in a language the customer reads, and record the choice. This is good practice; check whether a specific rule applies.
gates: **Residence list:** Decide which residence groups the app serves, block other residences by default, and get Legal sign-off on the list.
**Mainland advice:** Obtain written mainland advice before showing any product to a mainland resident.
**Statement build:** Build the Important Facts Statement step with the customer's acknowledgement and the record the IA requires (reported; check). Test the step for mainland visitors before release.
**Non-resident due diligence:** Confirm the bank's customer due diligence and risk rating for non-resident customers under Cap. 615 Sch. 2, and document the approach.

**Complaints route:** Agree how a complaint from an overseas customer reaches the insurer and the bank. Complaints about the bank's conduct as an agency go to the HKMA, and a personal policy-term or claims dispute with the insurer goes to the Insurance Complaints Bureau (reported; check its current scope).
**Insurer agreement:** Each insurer confirms in writing that it accepts applications from the chosen residence groups and will provide the service the bank promises.
**Service centre licensing:** If the bank uses Greater Bay Area service centres, Legal confirms the licensing and contract position first.
watchFor: **Default residence:** A form that defaults to a Hong Kong address can put a mainland customer into the wrong journey.
**Statement skipped:** A mainland visitor who reaches the application without the Important Facts Statement step may breach the IA's requirement (reported).

**Overseas advertising:** Marketing to the public from a place outside Hong Kong is treated as holding out under s.64H, so advertising run from mainland or Greater Bay Area premises needs its own analysis. Keep advertising to the approved residence groups.

activities.title: Promotions, gifts and rebates
activities.summary: App banners, premium rebates, gifts, cashback, referral rewards and push notifications all invite customers to buy. An invitation to enter a contract of insurance is a regulated activity under Schedule 1A, so promotions carry insurance conduct risk as well as marketing and data risk. The IA restricts gifts and rebates on some classes of business.
activities.route: Yes, for promotions that fit the rules. Gifts are restricted for Class C products, and rebates on long term policies are allowed only if they meet GL25's criteria, which reportedly include recording the rebate in the policy documents (reported; check para 6.2). Each offer needs Legal, compliance and product sign-off before it goes live.
require: **Invitations are regulated:** Schedule 1A Part 1, item 1(b) covers inviting or inducing a person to enter a contract of insurance. A banner or push notice that invites a purchase is a regulated act, not just marketing.

**Gifts:** IA Guideline GL25 on the offering of gifts, issued under s.133, bars gifts for Class C (linked long term) products when they are marketed, promoted or distributed. Interpretation notes allow more flexibility for some other classes (reported; check the current text).

**Premium rebates:** Under GL25, rebates on long term products are allowed only in the cases it sets out, including where the rebate is recorded in the policy documents (reported; check the criteria).

**Referral rewards:** s.64N(2) bars an authorized insurer from accepting a referral from a person who is not a licensed intermediary and whose duties are not only clerical or administrative. A breach is an offence under s.64N(5). The enforce-or-void right in s.64N(3) applies only to contracts made through an unlicensed person under s.64N(1).

**Referral fee circulars:** IA circulars on referral fees, including one of 1 September 2025 on fees paid by licensed broker companies for participating policies, focus on large fees and inducements (reported; check the benchmark).

**Direct marketing consent:** PDPO s.35E bars direct marketing with personal data unless the customer has consented after the s.35C notice. A breach is an offence, with a fine of HK$500,000 and 3 years' imprisonment on conviction.

**Premium financing offers:** A November 2025 HKMA circular reportedly stresses separating premium financing from insurance applications and bars return-enhancing promotions (reported; check the original).
gates: **Promotion register:** Log each offer with its product class, value, conditions and type (gift, rebate, cashback, referral reward or banner).
**Class check:** Confirm the class of each product in an offer, and block gifts on Class C products.
**Rebate wording:** Put any rebate terms in the policy documents, schedule or quotation before the offer goes live.

**Referrer licensing:** Pay referral rewards only to licensed intermediaries, or to persons whose duties for the bank only involve clerical or administrative work, as s.64N(2) requires. Check each partner, app or influencer before it earns a reward.
**Consent check:** Confirm opt-in consent and the s.35C notice for every push, email or in-app campaign that uses personal data.
**Premium financing separation:** Keep premium financing offers out of the insurance application journey, and check the wording for return-enhancing terms.
**Review record:** Legal, compliance and product sign off each offer, and the sign-off is kept on file.
watchFor: **Cashback as rebate:** A cashback or points reward on a policy can work as an undisclosed rebate. Check it against GL25 before launch.
**Banner to buy:** A banner that links straight to an application is an invitation. It needs the same disclosure and needs-analysis steps as any other sale.
**Unlicensed partners:** Partner apps or influencers paid per sale may be unlicensed referrers under s.64N(2), which is an offence for the insurer.

activities.title: Renewals, claims help, surrender and replacement
activities.summary: After the sale, customers ask for help to renew, surrender, claim or replace a policy. These are material decisions under Schedule 1A Part 2, so inducing a customer to make one, or advising on one, is a regulated activity. Replacement is restricted by IA guidance, and the bank must account properly for any client money that passes through it.
activities.route: Yes, through the same licensed agency or broker, with each after-sale task mapped to that licence. Reminders and forwarding can be administrative, but advice on surrender, replacement or a claim needs a licensed adviser, and the bank should not assess or settle claims.
require: **Material decisions:** Schedule 1A Part 2 lists the making of an application, renewal, surrender, exercise of a right, change of terms and settlement of a claim as material decisions (s.3A(b)). Inducing or advising on them is regulated under Parts 1 and 3.

**Administrative exception:** s.123(2) does not prohibit clerical or administrative work for an intermediary. Forwarding documents, tracking status and sending reminders may fall within it. Anything that assesses a claim or advises on a decision does not.

**Claims business:** s.123(1)(g) lets a loss assessor or claims settler give regulated advice in that business. It gives no such exception to a bank. Keep the bank clear of advice on claims, and do not settle claims for insurers unless Legal confirms the position.

**Replacement:** IA Guideline GL27 covers replacement of long term policies, and IA interpretation notes of 22 September 2020 cover GL27 with GL25 (reported; check the current text). A suggested switch needs a comparison and proper disclosure.

**Client money:** s.90(h) requires the assets of the policy holder to be promptly and properly accounted for. Refunds, surrender values and claim payments routed through the bank need tracking and reconciliation.

**Surrender disclosure:** s.90(e) requires enough disclosure for the customer to be sufficiently informed before a surrender decision. Showing the surrender value and any charges before the request is processed is the practical way to meet it (good practice).

**Complaints routing:** Agree with each insurer where a complaint about a policy goes first, and check the Insurance Complaints Bureau's current scope and limit before writing the routing down. Complaints about the bank's own conduct as an agency go to the HKMA (reported).
gates: **Task map:** Map each after-sale task as administrative, regulated or insurer-only, with the licence that covers it.
**Replacement control:** A replacement is suggested only after a comparison and a GL27 check, approved by compliance.
**Claims boundary:** Confirm the bank does not assess or settle claims, or that a licensed claims service handles them under its own authority.
**Money flow:** Map each payment that passes through a bank account, with separate accounting, reconciliation and a named owner for each flow.
**Complaints route:** Agree with each insurer how complaints are routed, how quickly, and what the bank tells the customer while they wait.
**Renewal messages:** Check that renewal and surrender messages inform without inviting a change to terms, since an invitation is a regulated act under Schedule 1A Part 1.
**Insurer contracts:** Each insurer confirms how renewals, surrender requests and claim intake work, and who keeps the record.
watchFor: **Helpful switch:** A service agent who says 'switch to the new plan' is inviting a replacement, which needs the GL27 check first.
**Claims creep:** A help desk that reviews claim documents and gives a view on the outcome has moved into assessing claims.
**Money in transit:** A surrender value or refund sitting in a bank account while the customer waits is client money under s.90(h).

title: Authorized insurers: the bank's partner
oneLiner: An authorized insurer carries the legal risk for its agents, so the bank must diligence the insurer as closely as the product.
keyPoints: **Authorization:** An insurer needs written authorization from the Insurance Authority (IA) under s.8 for long term or general business, or under s.8A for [[special purpose insurer]] business. The IA must refuse if a director or controller is not fit and proper.

**Register:** The IA keeps a register of authorized insurers, showing each insurer's classes and any restricting conditions (s.5H). Anyone may inspect it free of charge at all reasonable times, and the IA must make it available online as far as practicable.

**People:** An insurer may appoint a controller only with IA approval (s.13A). A director of an HK or designated insurer (s.13AC), or a key person in control functions of a non-captive insurer (s.13AE), also needs approval. The IA tests each person against the fit and proper criteria in s.14A.
**Agents:** The insurer is liable for acts of its appointed agent in dealings with clients, subject to narrow exceptions (s.68). It may contract only through licensed intermediaries (s.64N).
**Intervention:** Part V gives the IA powers to restrict new business and require assets and investments to be held. Part VA lets it revoke or suspend authorization (s.41P), after a hearing (s.41Q).
**Counsel's role:** Treat the insurer's approvals, register entry and capital position as due diligence items. Write the agency agreement around the insurer's liability.
