deepDive.heading: Marketing in the app and social media
deepDive.lede: An app invitation to buy insurance is a regulated activity, even when it looks like a banner.
points: **Invitations are regulated:** Inviting or inducing a person to enter a contract of insurance is a regulated activity (Sch. 1A, Pt 1, item 1(b)). Section 64G(1) prohibits carrying it on in the course of business or for reward, subject to the exceptions in s.64G(3) and s.123.
**Exception does not help:** The s.123(1)(f)(iii) exception covers advice, not promotion. Banners, product pages and push notifications need a licensing analysis.
**Referrals:** An authorized insurer must not accept a referral from a person in Hong Kong unless that person is licensed or only does clerical work (s.64N(2)). A breach is an offence (s.64N(5)).
**Affiliates and influencers:** A paid promoter who recommends or invites purchase may be carrying on a regulated activity. Control scripts, disclosures and tracking links.
**Gifts:** GL25 is reported to bar gifts to customers when marketing Class C products. Check the current text.
deepDive.takeaway: Treat every promotion, referral link and influencer post as a regulated activity until counsel clears it.

provisions.title: Conduct requirements for licensed insurance agencies and their responsible officers
provisions.summary: A licensed agency must keep controls for compliance with the conduct requirements by itself and its licensed technical representatives, and must use best endeavours to secure observance. Its responsible officer must use best endeavours to ensure those controls exist and are observed.
provisions.counselNote: This is the core allocation for an app sale. The bank, if it is the agency, cannot delegate the duty to software or to the insurer.

provisions.title: Exceptions to sections 64G and 120
provisions.summary: Section 64G does not prohibit regulated advice given through electronic communication to the public. The exception covers giving advice, and does not refer to inviting, inducing or arranging.
provisions.counselNote: Use this as a narrow point, not as a design basis for an app flow that leads to purchase.

provisions.title: Power to conduct inspection
provisions.summary: An IA inspector may enter business premises, inspect and copy business records, and make inquiries of a licensed insurance intermediary. The inspector may also require production of records and answers about them.
provisions.counselNote: The app's logs, versions and consent records are business records. Keep them retrievable from day one.

provisions.title: Production of information in information systems, etc.
provisions.summary: Where a required record is recorded in a form that is not legible, the power to require production includes power to require a legible reproduction, including from an information system.
provisions.counselNote: Database and log design must allow a readable reproduction of any past sale.

provisions.title: Contracts of insurance made through persons other than licensed insurance intermediaries, etc.
provisions.summary: An authorized insurer must not contract through, or accept a referral from, a person in Hong Kong unless that person is licensed or only does clerical or administrative work. Contravention is an offence, and a contract made in breach can be enforced by or voided at the policy holder's option.
provisions.counselNote: Affiliate, referral and influencer schemes must be checked against this section before launch.

provisions.title: Regulated Activity, Material Decision and Regulated Advice
provisions.summary: Regulated activities include negotiating or arranging a contract of insurance, inviting or inducing a person to enter one, inviting or inducing a material decision, and giving regulated advice.
provisions.counselNote: Marketing that invites a purchase is regulated even where no advice is given.

provisions.title: Data user must not use personal data in direct marketing without data subject's consent
provisions.summary: A data user who has complied with s.35C must not use personal data in direct marketing without consent matching the information given, consistent with the permitted kind of data and class of marketing subjects. A breach is an offence with a fine of $500,000 and 3 years' imprisonment on conviction.
provisions.counselNote: Cross-selling insurance from banking data needs consent that names insurance products and the right class of marketing.

provisions.title: Data Protection Principles
provisions.summary: Personal data must be collected for a lawful purpose, adequate but not excessive, by fair means. The data subject must be told whether supply is obligatory and the consequences of not supplying it.
provisions.counselNote: Each app form field needs a purpose and a notice. Health questions must be necessary for the product.

provisions.title: Prohibition against transfer of personal data to place outside Hong Kong except in specified circumstances
provisions.summary: Section 33 would restrict transfers of personal data outside Hong Kong unless one of its conditions applies. It is reported as not yet in force, so check its commencement on eLegislation.
provisions.counselNote: Check the status on eLegislation and the vendor map. Plan for the current data protection principles either way.

provisions.title: Electronic signatures, digital signatures, etc.
provisions.summary: An electronic signature satisfies a signing requirement if the signer uses a method that identifies them and shows approval, the method is reliable and appropriate in the circumstances, and the other party consents to the method.
provisions.counselNote: Record the customer's consent to the e-signature method and keep the reliability assessment.

provisions.title: Guideline on the Use of Internet for Insurance Activities
provisions.summary: Reported to apply to insurers, intermediaries and other regulated groups doing insurance business online. Reported points include accurate, current sales materials and client identity checks. Check the current text.
provisions.counselNote: Obtain and read the full text before the design freeze. The points here are reported and need checking against it.

provisions.title: Guideline on Cybersecurity
provisions.summary: Issued under s.133(1) and revised with effect from 1 January 2025. It applies to authorized insurers. Reported to require notice of reportable cyber incidents to the IA within 72 hours of detection.
provisions.counselNote: Bind the insurer partner to its GL20 duties in the contract. The bank's own duties must be checked separately.

checklist: **Name the licensed agency** for app sales and confirm who the responsible officer is (s.91(2)).
**Map each app step** to a legal duty, a control and an owner. Keep the map with the journey versions.
**Record consent** for each marketing use and each insurer data share under PDPO Part 6A.
**Test the e-signature method** against ETO s.6(1)(c)-(e) and record the customer's consent to it.
**Confirm the current IA status** of video or remote sales guidance before launch.
**Test the advice engine** and log its versions, inputs and outputs.
**Agree incident notices** with the insurer, including who notifies the IA and within what time.
**Review referral links, affiliates and influencers** against s.64N(2) before any campaign.
itAngle: **Journey logging:** Log each screen version, disclosure and consent with a timestamp and a reference. This is the record the IA may inspect under s.64ZZF.
**Legibility:** Store records in a form that can be reproduced in legible form (s.64ZZS). Test retrieval of a past sale on a schedule.
**Signing:** Use an e-signature method that is reliable and consented to (ETO s.6(1)). Keep the reliability assessment with the product file.
**Interfaces:** Each insurer API needs a data map, access controls and monitoring. The bank's and the insurer's control sets may differ, so document the gap.
bankNotes: **Existing controls:** The bank already works under HKMA technology risk and outsourcing expectations (SPM modules TM-G-1 and SA-2; check current versions). Map the insurance journey into them rather than building a second set.
**Data sharing:** Sharing customer data with insurer partners needs PDPO consent (Part 6A) and a separate banking secrecy analysis.
**Two supervisors:** The HKMA supervises the bank and the IA regulates the sale. Expect both to ask about the same journey and the same records.
**Video sales:** The HKMA's December 2024 circular on video-conference sales is directly relevant to a bank that sells through video. Read it with the IA's position.
pitfalls: **Using the advice exception as a design basis:** s.123(1)(f)(iii) covers advice only. Arranging or inviting stays regulated (Sch. 1A, Pt 1, item 1).
**Assuming implied e-consent:** ETO s.6(1)(e) requires the other party's consent to the method. Silence is not consent.
**Blanket marketing consent:** s.35E(1) requires consent that matches the permitted kind of data and class of marketing subjects. A general opt-in may not be enough.
**Assuming one incident clock:** The reported GL20 notice period for insurers is separate from the bank's HKMA timing. Each clock runs on its own rule.

glossary.definition: An individual approved by the IA under s.64ZE as the agency's responsible officer, who must use best endeavours to ensure the agency's conduct controls exist and are observed (s.91(2)).

An act listed in Sch. 1A, Pt 1 of Cap. 41, such as arranging a contract of insurance or inviting a person to enter one. Carrying one on in the course of business or for reward needs a licence (s.64G).

Offering goods, services or facilities, or soliciting donations, by sending information or goods addressed to specific persons by name, or by calling them. PDPO Part 6A sets consent rules for using and sharing personal data for this purpose.

Data attached to or associated with an electronic record to identify the signer and show approval. Under ETO s.6 it satisfies a signing requirement if the method is reliable and the other party consents.
Cap. 41 does not define this phrase. Section 123(1)(f)(iii) lists it as one channel through which regulated advice may be given without breaching s.64G.
A record of a licensed intermediary's business that an IA inspector may inspect, copy and require to be produced under s.64ZZF.
The six principles in Schedule 1 to the PDPO covering collection, accuracy, retention, use, security, openness and access.
A cyber incident that GL20 requires an authorized insurer to report to the IA. The definition and thresholds should be read in the full guideline.

title: AML/CFT for insurance
oneLiner: A bank that sells insurance is a financial institution under AMLO, so policy CDD, records and suspicious transaction reports fall on it.
keyPoints: **Who is caught:** AMLO treats authorized insurers, licensed individual insurance agents, licensed insurance agencies and licensed insurance broker companies as financial institutions (Sch. 1, Pt 2). An authorized institution is one too.

**Scope limits:** Schedule 2 applies to an authorized insurer only for long term business (s.5(2)). For agents, agencies and brokers it applies only to transactions in the classes named in Cap. 41, Sch. 1, Pt 2 (s.5(3)).

**Policy-specific CDD:** A named beneficiary must be recorded when designated. A beneficiary described by class must be identified before the earlier of exercise of rights or first payout, and verified then (Sch. 2, s.11).
**Reliance:** An institution may carry out CDD through a specified intermediary that consents in writing and supplies copies on request. It stays liable for any failure (Sch. 2, s.18).
**Records and monitoring:** Keep CDD and transaction records for at least five years and monitor the relationship continuously (Sch. 2, ss.5 and 20).

**Reporting:** Knowledge or suspicion of proceeds of crime must be disclosed as soon as reasonable (OSCO s.25A(1), DTROP s.25A). Knowledge or suspicion of terrorist property must be disclosed as soon as practicable (UNATMO s.12(1)). [[Tipping off]] is a separate offence.

conceptMap.caption: How CDD, monitoring and reporting run in sequence for one policy.

deepDive.heading: Who the regime catches
deepDive.lede: Insurance intermediaries are financial institutions, but how far Schedule 2 reaches depends on the role the bank plays.

visual.caption: Scope depends on the role and the product class, not only on the licence.

items.label: Authorized insurer
items.note: Schedule 2 applies to long term business only (s.5(2))

items.label: Licensed insurance agency
items.note: Applies to transactions in the Cap. 41 column 3 classes (s.5(3))

items.label: Bank as authorized institution
items.note: Full Schedule 2 for its banking business

points: **Definition:** AMLO Sch. 1, Pt 2 defines financial institution to include authorized insurers, licensed individual insurance agents, licensed insurance agencies and licensed insurance broker companies, alongside authorized institutions.
**Insurer scope:** Schedule 2 applies to an authorized insurer only in relation to long term business, which has the meaning given in Cap. 41, s.2(1) (s.5(2) and (11)).

**Intermediary scope:** For agents, agencies and brokers, Schedule 2 applies only to transactions involving the contracts described in column 3 of Cap. 41, Sch. 1, Pt 2 (s.5(3)). Check each product against those classes before relying on the scope.
**Bank as agency:** When the bank sells as a licensed insurance agency, it is a financial institution for those transactions as well as an authorized institution for its banking business.

**Relevant authority:** The Insurance Authority (IA) is the relevant authority for insurers and licensed intermediaries. For an authorized institution it is the Monetary Authority, which the HKMA exercises in practice (AMLO Sch. 1, Pt 2).
deepDive.takeaway: Map each insurance transaction to the bank's role before deciding which AML duties apply.

deepDive.heading: CDD for policy holders and beneficiaries
deepDive.lede: A policy adds a beneficiary step that a bank account does not have.

visual.caption: Beneficiary checks run at designation, then again at the payout event.

items.label: Named beneficiary
items.note: Record the name (s.11(1)(a))

items.label: Described beneficiary
items.note: Exercise of rights or first payout (s.11(1)(b))

items.label: Verification
items.note: Reliable documents; identify beneficial owners of a legal person or trust, and verify them if the risk is high (s.11(3)(b))

points: **Customer CDD:** Identify and verify the customer on reliable, independent documents, and identify and verify any beneficial owner (Sch. 2, s.2).

**Timing:** CDD is due before a business relationship starts, or before an occasional transaction of HK$120,000 or more (Sch. 2, s.3(1)(a) and (b)). Verification may follow the start of the relationship where delay would interrupt business and the risk is managed, but it must be completed as soon as reasonably practicable (s.3(2)-(3)).
**Named beneficiaries:** Record the name when the policy holder identifies the beneficiary (Sch. 2, s.11(1)(a)).

**Described beneficiaries:** Where the beneficiary is designated by description or other means, obtain enough information to establish identity by the earlier of exercise of rights or first payout (s.11(1)(b) and (2)).

**Payout checks:** At exercise or payout, verify the beneficiary's identity from documents from a governmental body or other reliable source. For a legal person or trust, identify the beneficial owners (s.11(3)).
deepDive.takeaway: Build beneficiary capture into the policy journey, not only into onboarding.

deepDive.heading: Intermediaries and reliance
deepDive.lede: CDD can be carried out through another regulated firm, but the relying firm keeps the liability.

visual.caption: Reliance is permitted on written terms, and liability does not move to the intermediary.

centre.label: Relying institution
centre.note: Bank or insurer relying on CDD

items.label: Specified intermediary
items.rel: consents in writing to act for

points: **Reliance:** An institution may carry out a CDD measure through an intermediary only if the intermediary consents in writing and will provide copies on request (Sch. 2, s.18(1)).

**Specified intermediaries:** The list includes authorized institutions, licensed corporations, authorized insurers, licensed individual insurance agents, licensed insurance agencies and licensed insurance broker companies (s.18(3)(b)).
**Liability stays:** The relying institution remains liable under the Ordinance for any failure to carry out the CDD measure (s.18(2)).
**Data flow:** Obtain the intermediary's data immediately after it completes the measure, and make sure copies can be obtained within the record-keeping period (s.18(4)(a) and (b)).
deepDive.takeaway: Write the reliance terms into the bank-insurer agreement: written consent, copy access on request and a time limit.

deepDive.heading: Ongoing monitoring and records
deepDive.lede: AML duties continue after the sale, and the file must be kept for years.
points: **Continuous monitoring:** Review CDD information from time to time and scrutinise transactions for consistency with the institution's knowledge of the customer (Sch. 2, s.5(1)).
**Review triggers:** CDD must be repeated when the institution suspects money laundering or terrorist financing, or doubts earlier information (Sch. 2, s.3(1)(d) and (e)).

**Red flags to watch:** Early surrender or cancellation, third-party premium payers and beneficiary changes close to a payout. These are good-practice indicators, not statutory lists. Compare them with the IA's current examples before finalising the monitoring rules.
**Retention:** Transaction records are kept for at least five years. Customer records are kept throughout the relationship and for at least five years after it ends (Sch. 2, s.20(1)–(3)).
deepDive.takeaway: Set the retention clock at policy inception and diarise reviews for surrender and beneficiary events.

deepDive.heading: Reporting, tipping off and sanctions
deepDive.lede: Suspicion creates a legal duty to report, and disclosing the report to the customer is an offence.

visual.caption: The escalation path is one-way: from suspicion to disclosure, without any word to the customer.

items.label: Suspicion arises
items.note: Knows or suspects proceeds or terrorist property

items.label: Internal escalation
items.note: Use the bank's procedure (OSCO s.25A(4))

items.label: Disclosure
items.note: To an authorized officer, as soon as reasonable

items.label: No tipping off
items.note: Nothing likely to prejudice an investigation

points: **Duty to disclose:** A person who knows or suspects that property represents proceeds of an indictable offence must disclose it to an authorized officer as soon as reasonable (OSCO s.25A(1), Cap. 455).
**Drug proceeds:** The same duty applies under DTROP s.25A (Cap. 405) for drug trafficking proceeds. The text shown is dated 2019, so check the current text before relying on it.
**Terrorist property:** UNATMO s.12(1) requires disclosure to an authorized officer, as soon as practicable, of knowledge or suspicion that property is terrorist property (Cap. 575).
**Protected disclosure:** A disclosure is not a breach of contractual confidence and does not create liability in damages for the disclosure itself (OSCO s.25A(3)).

**Tipping off:** Telling another person something likely to prejudice an investigation after a disclosure is an offence (OSCO s.25A(5)), with a maximum of HK$500,000 and three years on indictment (s.25A(8)(a)).
**Failure to report:** Not making a required disclosure is an offence, punishable by a fine at level 5 and three months' imprisonment (OSCO s.25A(7)).

provisions.instrument: Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Ordinance (Cap. 615)
provisions.title: Schedule 2 has effect with respect to financial institutions
provisions.summary: Schedule 2 applies to financial institutions. Its reach is narrowed for authorized insurers (long term business only) and for agents, agencies and brokers (transactions in named classes). Knowing contravention of a specified provision is an offence.
provisions.counselNote: Confirm the bank's role for each product before applying Schedule 2. Penalties for knowing breach reach staff too (s.5(7)), so training matters.

provisions.instrument: Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Ordinance (Cap. 615)
provisions.title: Interpretation
provisions.summary: Defines financial institution to include authorized institutions, authorized insurers, licensed individual insurance agents, licensed insurance agencies and licensed insurance broker companies. The relevant authority is the IA for insurers and intermediaries, and the Monetary Authority for authorized institutions.
provisions.counselNote: The definition explains why the bank is caught twice, once as an authorized institution and once as an agency, and that the IA and HKMA each supervise a part.

provisions.instrument: Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Ordinance (Cap. 615)
provisions.title: What are customer due diligence measures
provisions.summary: Sets out the CDD measures: identify and verify the customer on reliable, independent documents or data, and identify and verify beneficial owners. The measures apply to financial institutions and specified DNFBPs.
provisions.counselNote: The policy holder is the customer. Identify and verify the holder before the policy starts, using sources the statute accepts.

provisions.instrument: Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Ordinance (Cap. 615)
provisions.title: When customer due diligence measures must be carried out
provisions.summary: CDD must be carried out before a business relationship is established, and before an occasional transaction of HK$120,000 or more, whether it is one operation or several linked ones.
provisions.counselNote: A policy purchase normally creates a business relationship, so CDD is due before the policy starts under s.3(1)(a). The HK$120,000 occasional-transaction limb applies only to a transaction with a customer who has no business relationship with the bank or insurer.

provisions.instrument: Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Ordinance (Cap. 615)
provisions.title: Special requirements for insurance policies
provisions.summary: Requires the institution to record a named beneficiary, or to obtain enough information about a described beneficiary, by the earlier of exercise of rights or first payout. At that time the beneficiary's identity must be verified from reliable sources, and beneficial owners identified if the beneficiary is a legal person or trust.
provisions.counselNote: The product team must capture beneficiary data at designation, and the operations team must run a verification step before any payout.

provisions.instrument: Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Ordinance (Cap. 615)
provisions.title: Carrying out customer due diligence measures by means of intermediaries
provisions.summary: Allows CDD to be carried out through a specified intermediary that consents in writing and will provide copies on request. The relying institution remains liable, must obtain the intermediary's data promptly and must ensure copies are available within the record-keeping period.
provisions.counselNote: Reliance is the core contract term between the bank and any insurer or agency. Draft consent, copy access and time limits into the agreement.

provisions.instrument: Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Ordinance (Cap. 615)
provisions.title: Duty to keep records
provisions.summary: Requires records of each transaction and of customer identification and account files to be kept. Transaction records are kept for at least five years. Customer records are kept throughout the relationship and for at least five years after it ends.
provisions.counselNote: The retention period runs from the relationship end, so policies that last decades need a long-running retention plan. The IA may also extend retention by written notice for a specified customer or transaction (Sch. 2, s.20(4)).

provisions.title: Disclosure of knowledge or suspicion that property represents proceeds, etc. of indictable offence
provisions.summary: Requires disclosure to an authorized officer, as soon as reasonable, of knowledge or suspicion that property represents proceeds of an indictable offence. Disclosure is protected from contractual and damages claims. Tipping off and failure to report are offences.
provisions.counselNote: The reporting duty is personal, so the bank's internal escalation process must be documented and fast enough to meet the as-soon-as-reasonable test.

provisions.title: Disclosure of knowledge or suspicion that property represents proceeds, etc. of drug trafficking
provisions.summary: Parallel duty to disclose knowledge or suspicion that property is linked to drug trafficking, with the same tipping-off offence structure as OSCO s.25A.
provisions.counselNote: The text shown is dated 19 September 2019, so confirm it is the current version before quoting penalties.

provisions.title: Disclosure of knowledge or suspicion that property is terrorist property, etc.
provisions.summary: Requires a person who knows or suspects that property is terrorist property to disclose the information to an authorized officer as soon as practicable.
provisions.counselNote: Terrorist-property reports run alongside the OSCO route, so one case file may need both analyses. The text shown is as at 20 June 2019, so confirm it is the current version before quoting it.

provisions.ref: GL3 (2023 revision, gazetted to take effect 1 June 2023). A further revision was issued by circular dated 30 May 2025; check its commencement date and the current text before relying on this entry.
provisions.title: Anti-money laundering and counter-terrorist financing guideline (GL3)
provisions.summary: The IA's AML/CFT guideline gives guidance on Schedule 2 under AMLO s.7 and Cap. 41 s.133. Its application to licensed insurance agencies and broker companies should be checked in the current text.
provisions.counselNote: Read the current GL3 before designing the insurance AML process. A breach of GL3 does not by itself create liability (AMLO s.7(4)), but GL3 is admissible in evidence, and the IA must have regard to it when it assesses a Schedule 2 contravention (s.7(4)-(5)).

provisions.instrument: HKMA Guideline on Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Financing of Terrorism (For Authorized Institutions)
provisions.title: Guideline on Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Financing of Terrorism (For Authorized Institutions)
provisions.summary: The HKMA guideline for authorized institutions under AMLO s.7 and Banking Ordinance s.7(3). The bank already follows it for its banking business, and it sets the standard the bank's group AML policy should meet.
provisions.counselNote: Use the HKMA guideline for the bank's account and card business. Check whether any later HKMA or HKAB FAQs on AML supplement it, and whether insurance sales add HKMA-specific expectations.

checklist: Confirm which of the bank's insurance roles (agency, broker or sale as an authorized institution) makes it a financial institution for each product.
Map each product to the AMLO s.5(2) and (3) scope: long term business, or the Cap. 41 column 3 classes.
Capture beneficiary names and identifiers at designation, and set a verification trigger for exercise or payout.
Put the Sch. 2, s.18 reliance terms into the insurer agreement: written consent, copy access and time limits.
Retain CDD and transaction records for at least five years under Sch. 2, s.20, and align retention with the insurer's systems.
Agree in writing who runs CDD, monitoring and STR decisions for a shared customer.
Train front-line staff so surrender and cancellation queries do not reveal a report (tipping off).
Check the current GL3 and HKMA guideline versions, and their scope for agencies, before sign-off.
itAngle: **Beneficiary data:** Capture beneficiary names and identifiers in the app at designation, and store the date on which verification is due.

**Screening:** Run sanctions and watch-list screening of policy holders and beneficiaries at onboarding and before payout. Sanctions duties under the UNSO (Cap. 537) and UNATMO (Cap. 575) should be confirmed with the bank's sanctions team.
**Records:** Hold CDD and transaction records for at least five years, with a secure route to supply copies to the insurer on request.
**Alerts:** Build monitoring rules for surrender, cancellation and beneficiary-change events, and route alerts into the STR workflow.
bankNotes: **One customer, two regimes:** A customer may hold a bank account and a policy. Each relationship needs its own CDD, but the customer file can be shared within the bank.
**Shared processes:** Plan one CDD process and one suspicion review for both, so the same red flags are not reviewed twice.

**Who files:** The duty falls on the person who knows or suspects, and an employee may report through the bank's or insurer's internal procedure (OSCO s.25A(4)). Agree in writing which entity files, and how the other is informed without breaching s.25A(5).

**Regulators:** The Monetary Authority is the relevant authority for the bank as an authorized institution. Where the bank acts as a licensed insurance agency, the IA is the relevant authority for those transactions (AMLO Sch. 1). Keep records for both ready for inspection.
pitfalls: **Assuming bank CDD covers the policy:** Beneficiary steps under Sch. 2, s.11 apply to the policy even where the holder is already a bank customer.
**Forgetting reliance liability:** Relying on an intermediary under s.18 does not transfer the liability for a failure (s.18(2)).
**Tipping off through service channels:** A surrender or cancellation query can reveal a report. Scripts and staff training must prevent this (OSCO s.25A(5)).

**Relying on an old guideline:** GL3 has been revised more than once (including by a circular dated 30 May 2025), and the HKMA guideline was revised in May 2023. Confirm the current versions before advising.

glossary.definition: The measures a financial institution takes to identify and verify a customer and any beneficial owner, and to monitor the relationship (Sch. 2, ss.2 and 5).
A person listed in AMLO Sch. 1, Pt 2, including authorized institutions, authorized insurers and licensed insurance intermediaries.
A person listed in Sch. 2, s.18(3) who may carry out CDD for another institution if the conditions in s.18 are met.
The person named or described in a policy to receive a benefit. Sch. 2, s.11 treats designation and payout as separate CDD trigger points.
Insurance business as defined in Cap. 41, s.2(1). AMLO applies to an authorized insurer only in relation to this business (s.5(2)).
A disclosure to an authorized officer when a person knows or suspects that property is proceeds of crime or terrorist property (OSCO s.25A; UNATMO s.12).
Disclosing to another person something likely to prejudice an investigation after a report has been made (OSCO s.25A(5)).
Continuous review of documents and transactions so that they remain consistent with the institution's knowledge of the customer (Sch. 2, s.5).

A transaction with a customer who has no business relationship with the institution (Sch. 2, s.1). CDD is due before it is carried out if it is HK$120,000 or more, alone or with linked transactions (s.3(1)(b)).

related.why: Insurer agreements must set the CDD reliance and record-sharing terms that s.18 requires.
Licence status determines which intermediary roles and AML duties apply to the bank.
App-based beneficiary capture and digital onboarding must meet the CDD steps in Sch. 2.
AML breaches carry separate disciplinary powers for the relevant authority under AMLO s.21.
Surrender and cancellation complaints create tipping-off risk if staff answer them carelessly.

title: Supervision, investigation & discipline
oneLiner: The IA can inspect, investigate and discipline intermediaries, and for a bank's insurance business it has delegated those powers to the Monetary Authority (s.4G).
keyPoints: **Two regulators:** The Insurance Authority (IA) sets the rules. The IA has delegated its inspection and investigation powers over authorized institutions' insurance business to the Monetary Authority (MA), a delegation in place since 23 September 2019 (s.4G; reported in IA and HKMA releases), and the IA can still act itself (s.4G(5)).
**Inspection:** Inspectors may enter business premises at reasonable times, copy business records and make inquiries (s.64ZZF). Customer information is subject to the limits in s.64ZZJ.

**Investigation:** The IA may direct staff or appoint investigators on stated grounds, including suspected misconduct (s.64ZZH). It must consult the MA before acting on an authorized institution or its staff or agents.

**Discipline:** Under s.81 the IA may revoke or suspend a licence, bar future applications, reprimand, or impose a pecuniary penalty of up to the greater of HK$10 million and three times the profit gained or loss avoided.
**Due process:** The IA must give a reasonable opportunity to be heard, give written reasons, and consult the MA before disciplining an authorized institution or its staff or agents (s.82).
**Counsel's role:** Know which regulator will attend, keep records ready to produce, and diarise the 21-day window to challenge a decision in the Insurance Appeals Tribunal.

deepDive.heading: Inspection: who looks and what they can see
deepDive.lede: Inspection is the routine route by which the regulator checks compliance. For a bank's insurance business, the IA has delegated its inspection powers to the Monetary Authority, a delegation in place since 23 September 2019 (s.4G; reported in IA and HKMA releases), so the MA is the regulator at the door, though the IA can still act itself (s.4G(5)).

visual.caption: Under delegation, the MA exercises inspection powers over an authorized institution's insurance business.

items.label: IA (Cap. 41)
items.note: Appoints inspectors in writing (s.64ZZF(6))

items.label: HKMA as MA
items.note: Exercises delegated powers for the bank's insurance business

points: **Inspector powers:** An inspector may enter business premises at any reasonable time, inspect and copy business records, and make inquiries (s.64ZZF(2)-(3)).
**Reach:** Business premises include those of the principal that appoints an agent, so records held by the insurer or agency can be in scope (s.64ZZF(10)).

**Delegation:** With Chief Executive in Council approval, the IA may delegate its inspection and investigation powers to the MA for a regulated activity carried on by an authorized institution (s.4G(1)). The IA may still act itself (s.4G(5)). The IA has made such a delegation, in place since 23 September 2019 (reported in IA and HKMA releases).

**Customer information:** An inspector may not require an authorized institution to disclose customer records unless the inspector is a specified authority, or certifies in writing that disclosure is necessary (s.64ZZJ(1)).
**Practical point:** Confirm with the HKMA which supervisory team covers insurance business, and map which insurance records sit with the bank, the insurer and the agency.

deepDive.heading: Investigation: from direction to evidence
deepDive.lede: An investigation is more formal than an inspection and carries stronger compulsory powers, subject to safeguards.

visual.caption: Escalation from a routine inspection to a court-authorized search. Each step needs a stated trigger.

items.label: Inspection
items.note: Routine access and records

items.label: Investigation
items.note: Reasonable cause needed; consult the MA if a bank, its staff or agent is involved (s.64ZZH(2)).

items.label: Warrant
items.note: Magistrate authorizes entry by force if needed

items.label: Prosecution
items.note: Offences for non-compliance and false records

points: **Grounds:** The IA may investigate where it has reasonable cause to believe a provision may have been contravened, that a person may have been involved in misconduct, or that a regulated activity is not in policy holders' or the public's interest (s.64ZZH(1)(a)-(c)).
**Consultation:** Before directing its staff or appointing an investigator on an authorized institution, or on its employee or agent, the IA must consult the MA (s.64ZZH(2)).

**Investigator powers:** An investigator may require documents, explanations, attendance for questions and written answers, and may demand customer information only on the conditions in s.64ZZJ(2) (s.64ZZH(6)).
**Warrants:** A magistrate may authorize entry, by force if necessary, within 7 days of the warrant, to search for and seize relevant records (s.64ZZP(1)-(2)).

**Self-incrimination:** If a person claims before answering that the answer might incriminate them, the answer is not admissible in most criminal proceedings. This does not cover offences under s.64ZZL(1)-(5), Part V of the Crimes Ordinance (Cap. 200), or perjury (s.64ZZM(2), (3)). Incrimination is no excuse for refusing to comply (s.64ZZL(6)).

deepDive.heading: Discipline: grounds, sanctions and procedure
deepDive.lede: Discipline turns a finding into a sanction, and the Ordinance sets a fixed sequence the IA must follow.

visual.caption: The statutory sequence before a s.81 sanction takes effect.

items.label: Opportunity to be heard
items.note: Written or oral representations

items.label: MA consulted
items.note: Required for an authorized institution or its staff or agents

items.label: Written notice with reasons
items.note: States reasons, effective time and terms

items.label: Sanction
items.note: Licence, reprimand, prohibition or penalty

items.label: Publication
items.note: The IA may publish details and reasons

points: **Grounds:** The IA may act if a person is or was guilty of misconduct as a regulated person, or was not a fit and proper person (s.81(1)). Misconduct includes breach of the Ordinance or licence conditions, and prejudicial conduct (s.80(1)).
**Who is caught:** Regulated persons include licensed insurance intermediaries, responsible officers, and persons concerned in the management of an agency or broker company (s.80(1)).

**Sanctions:** The IA may revoke or suspend a licence, revoke or suspend a responsible officer's approval, prohibit future applications or appointments, and reprimand privately or publicly (s.81(4)(a)-(d)).
**Penalty cap:** A pecuniary penalty may not exceed the greater of HK$10,000,000 and three times the profit gained or loss avoided (s.81(4)(e)).
**Penalty guidelines:** The IA must publish penalty guidelines in the Gazette, after consulting the MA, and have regard to them (s.83(1), (3)). Reported to be GL22 for regulated persons.

deepDive.heading: Conduct breaches and personal exposure
deepDive.lede: Breaches of the conduct rules do not by themselves found court proceedings (s.93(1)), but other liabilities are preserved (s.93(2)). Discipline is the main regulatory route, and it reaches the people who run the business.
points: **Not actionable by itself:** A failure to comply with the conduct requirements in ss.90-92 does not by itself create liability to judicial proceedings (s.93(1)). Other liabilities, such as at common law, are preserved (s.93(2)).

**Responsible officer duty:** The responsible officer must use best endeavours to ensure the agency has proper controls and procedures, and that they are observed by its licensed technical representatives (s.91(2)).
**Agency duty:** The agency must give its responsible officer sufficient authority, resources and support for that role (s.91(1)(c)-(d)).

**Personal exposure:** Misconduct by an agency can be attributed to its responsible officers, or to persons concerned in management of its regulated activities, where they consented, connived or were negligent (s.80(3)-(4)). The same applies to broker companies (s.80(5)-(6)).

**Bank note:** A bank's own sales staff should be licensed and supervised within the conduct framework, so that a breach does not become a personal sanction for an individual with no controls behind them.

deepDive.heading: Appeals: the Insurance Appeals Tribunal
deepDive.lede: A disciplined person has a statutory route to challenge the decision, but the time limit is short.

visual.caption: The review window runs from service of the decision notice.

items.label: Decision notice served
items.note: Notice informs the person of the decision

items.label: Application for review due
items.note: Written, with grounds (s.100(1)-(2))

items.label: Extension
items.note: Only for good cause, after hearing both sides (s.100(4)-(5))

points: **Tribunal:** Part XII establishes the Insurance Appeals Tribunal (s.97). It reviews the specified decisions listed in Sch. 9.
**Time limit:** An application must be made in writing within 21 days after the notice of the decision is served (s.100(1)). The Tribunal may extend time for good cause (s.100(4)-(5)).
**Grounds:** The application must state its grounds (s.100(2)).

**Further appeal:** A party may appeal to the Court of Appeal on a question of law, fact or mixed law and fact, but only with leave (s.112(1)-(2), (4)). Otherwise the Tribunal's determination is final, subject to s.50 of the High Court Ordinance (Cap. 4) and s.112 (s.115).

**Effect pending review:** An application for review does not by itself stay the decision (s.110(1)). A stay may be sought from the Tribunal (s.110(2)). If no review is applied for, the decision takes effect when the 21 days expire (s.116(1)(b)).

deepDive.heading: Criminal offences that matter to a bank
deepDive.lede: Some offences attach to failure to cooperate with inspectors and investigators, and to the handling of records.
points: **Non-compliance:** Failing, without reasonable excuse, to comply with a specified requirement is an offence. On indictment the maximum is HK$200,000 and one year (s.64ZZL(1), (8)).

**False information:** Intent to defraud, or knowingly or recklessly giving false or misleading information in purported compliance, carries up to HK$1,000,000 and seven or two years, depending on the limb (s.64ZZL(2)-(5), (9)-(10)).
**Records:** Destroying, falsifying or concealing a record, with intent to conceal facts from an inspector or investigator, carries up to HK$1,000,000 and two years on indictment (s.64ZZN(1)-(2)).
**Cost orders:** A court convicting on a prosecution that follows an investigation may order the person to pay the investigation costs (s.64ZZO(1)).

**Licence applications:** Knowingly or recklessly making a false or misleading statement in a licence or approval application is an offence, with a fine at level 5 and 6 months' imprisonment on summary conviction (s.64ZZE(1), (3)).

provisions.title: Power to conduct inspection
provisions.summary: Lets an appointed inspector check a licensed insurance intermediary's compliance. The inspector may enter business premises, inspect and copy records and ask questions, and may require records and answers. Customer information is subject to s.64ZZJ.
provisions.counselNote: The bank's insurance records, and those held by its insurer and agency, should be ready to produce on short notice. Brief staff on the inspector's powers before the first visit.

provisions.title: Delegation of certain powers of Authority to Monetary Authority
provisions.summary: Allows the IA, with Chief Executive in Council approval, to delegate its inspection and investigation powers to the MA for a regulated activity of an authorized institution. The IA may still act concurrently, and the delegation can be conditioned, varied or withdrawn.
provisions.counselNote: This is why the bank's insurance inspection and investigation powers sit with the HKMA as Monetary Authority under the delegation in place since 23 September 2019 (s.4G; reported in IA and HKMA releases), while the IA can still act itself (s.4G(5)). Confirm the current delegation and its conditions with the HKMA.

provisions.title: Power to conduct investigation
provisions.summary: Lets the IA direct staff or appoint investigators where it has reasonable cause to suspect a contravention, misconduct or conduct against policy holders' interests. The IA must consult the MA before acting on an authorized institution or its staff or agents.
provisions.counselNote: Expect the MA to be consulted before an investigation touches the bank. Counsel should ask the HKMA whether an investigation is contemplated before answering informal questions.

provisions.title: Inspection and investigation powers in relation to authorized institutions
provisions.summary: Limits inspectors and investigators from requiring an authorized institution to disclose customer information. Only a specified authority, which includes the MA or its appointee, may do so freely. Others need written certification of necessity.
provisions.counselNote: Customer data requests in an inspection should be routed through the bank's compliance team and checked for the certification required by this section.

provisions.title: Offences in relation to inspections and investigations
provisions.summary: Creates offences for failing to comply with specified requirements, for false or misleading information given in compliance, and for causing others to fail. Penalties range from fines and short imprisonment on summary conviction to seven years' imprisonment on indictment.
provisions.counselNote: The bank's staff who answer inspection questions should understand that a false or misleading answer, given recklessly, is an offence. Answer accurately and check facts before they are given.

provisions.title: Interpretation
provisions.summary: Defines misconduct, including contravention of the Ordinance, licence conditions and prejudicial regulated activity, and defines regulated person to include licensed intermediaries, responsible officers and managers of agencies and broker companies.
provisions.counselNote: Use these definitions to decide which bank staff, and which managers of the sales function, are regulated persons who can be disciplined personally.

provisions.title: Disciplinary action in respect of regulated persons
provisions.summary: Lets the IA revoke or suspend licences, revoke or suspend responsible officer approvals, bar future applications, reprimand and impose a pecuniary penalty of up to the greater of HK$10 million and three times the profit or loss avoided. It may publish details of decisions.
provisions.counselNote: Model worst-case exposure with the penalty cap in mind. Plan the communications position on publication, because the decision may be made public with its reasons.

provisions.title: Procedural requirements in respect of exercise of powers under section 81
provisions.summary: Requires a reasonable opportunity to be heard before a s.81 power is used, written notice with reasons, the effective time and the terms of the sanction, and consultation with the MA for an authorized institution or its staff or agents.
provisions.counselNote: On receiving a notice of intended action, respond in writing within the stated time. Ask the IA to confirm that the MA was consulted where the bank or its staff are affected.

provisions.title: Guidelines for exercise of power to impose pecuniary penalty under section 81
provisions.summary: Requires the IA to publish guidelines in the Gazette before imposing a pecuniary penalty, to have regard to them, and to consult the MA before publishing. The guidelines are not subsidiary legislation.
provisions.counselNote: Read the current penalty guideline when assessing exposure. Its factors shape how penalties are set and how much mitigation is worth.

provisions.title: Guideline on Exercising Power to Impose Pecuniary Penalty in Respect of Regulated Persons
provisions.summary: Reported to set out how the IA proposes to use its pecuniary penalty power over regulated persons, including intermediaries. It treats penalties as more serious than reprimands.
provisions.counselNote: Read the GL22 text, not the summaries, before advising on penalty exposure. Confirm its gazettal date and current version with the IA.

provisions.title: Breach of conduct requirements
provisions.summary: Provides that failure to comply with the conduct requirements in ss.90-92 does not by itself lead to judicial proceedings. It preserves other liabilities, including at common law.
provisions.counselNote: Conduct failures are primarily a regulatory matter, but customers may still rely on general civil liability. Keep both exposures in view when designing complaint handling.

provisions.title: Insurance Appeals Tribunal
provisions.summary: Establishes the Insurance Appeals Tribunal to review specified decisions. Applications must be made in writing within 21 days of service of the decision, with extensions for good cause. Further appeal lies to the Court of Appeal in limited terms.
provisions.counselNote: Diarise the 21-day deadline from the date the decision notice is served. Decide quickly whether to seek review, because the window is short and extension needs good cause.

checklist: **Map the regulator:** Confirm which body inspects the bank's insurance business today, whether the IA delegation applies, and who the HKMA contact is.
**Records register:** Keep a register of insurance business records, and where each is held by the bank, insurer and agency, so production can be met quickly.
**Customer data protocol:** Route any request for customer data through compliance and check for a s.64ZZJ certification before disclosure.
**Inspection readiness:** Run a mock inspection covering premises, records and staff questions, and brief the staff who will answer.
**Answer accuracy:** Require that answers to regulators are checked against records, because false or misleading answers can be offences under s.64ZZL.
**Early-warning process:** Escalate any suspected misconduct by an agent or staff member to compliance and legal at once, so the bank can decide how to engage the HKMA.
**Decision calendar:** Set a 21-day alert on any service of a decision notice, and identify who decides whether to seek review.
**Penalty exposure model:** Calculate potential penalties against the s.81(4)(e) cap and the GL22 factors, and agree the communications plan for publication under s.81(5).
itAngle: **Record retention:** Inspectors can require records to be produced within a time and at a place they specify (s.64ZZF(3)(b)), so systems must retrieve historical insurance records on demand.
**Access control on customer data:** Systems should separate customer data that may be disclosed under s.64ZZJ, with logs of who produced what and under which certificate.

**Tamper-evident audit trails:** Once an inspector or investigator has required a record, destroying, falsifying or concealing it to hide facts from them is an offence (s.64ZZN(1)). Deletion rules, retention schedules and audit logs need legal sign-off.
**Evidence handling for warrants:** A warrant can allow seizure within 7 days (s.64ZZP), so teams need an incident runbook that covers secure export and chain of custody.
bankNotes: **MA as inspector:** The IA has delegated its inspection and investigation powers over the bank's insurance business to the Monetary Authority, a delegation in place since 23 September 2019 (s.4G; reported in IA and HKMA releases), and the IA can still act itself (s.4G(5)). The HKMA relationship is therefore a main supervisory channel for insurance business.

**Consultation duties:** The IA must consult the MA before investigating or disciplining an authorized institution or its staff or agents (ss.64ZZH(2), 82(4)). The bank should expect the HKMA to be involved at each step.
**IA penalty guideline:** Penalty exposure is set by s.81(4)(e) and the GL22 framework. Counsel should read the current text, because the bank's size and profits affect the profit-based limb.

**Existing HKMA relationship:** The bank's current supervisory dialogue and examination findings shape how the HKMA will view insurance activity. Align the insurance programme with those existing commitments.
pitfalls: **Treating the IA as the only regulator:** The IA has delegated its inspection and investigation powers over the bank's insurance business to the HKMA as Monetary Authority (s.4G), a delegation in place since 23 September 2019 (reported in IA and HKMA releases). Missing this changes who must be briefed.
**Missing the 21-day window:** A decision notice starts a short clock for review (s.100(1)). Delay without a good cause makes extension difficult.
**Informal answers to inspectors:** Casual answers can be inaccurate. A false or misleading answer given recklessly is an offence (s.64ZZL(3), (9)).
**Assuming conduct breaches are only regulatory:** Discipline is the main route under s.93, but other civil liability is preserved (s.93(2)), so complaints and disciplinary matters can overlap.

glossary.definition: A person the IA appoints in writing to check a licensed insurance intermediary's compliance and to inspect its records (s.64ZZF(6)).
A person directed or appointed to investigate a suspected contravention or misconduct under s.64ZZH, with powers to require records and answers.

The regulator of authorized institutions under the Banking Ordinance (Cap. 155). Under s.4G, the IA has delegated its inspection and investigation powers over a bank's insurance business to the Monetary Authority, a delegation in place since 23 September 2019 (reported in IA and HKMA releases).
A licensed insurance intermediary, a responsible officer, or a person concerned in the management of an agency or broker company (s.80(1)).

Under s.80(1), a contravention of the Ordinance, of a licence term or condition, or an act or omission in a regulated activity that the IA opines is, or is likely to be, prejudicial to policy holders or the public interest.
The standard the IA applies to regulated persons when deciding whether they may keep a licence or approval (s.81(1)(c)).
A fine the IA may impose on a regulated person. Capped at the greater of HK$10 million and three times the profit gained or loss avoided (s.81(4)(e)).
The tribunal established by Part XII to review specified decisions of the IA, on written application within 21 days.

related.why: The perimeter determines which activities are regulated, and so which conduct and investigation powers can be engaged.
The delegation of inspection and investigation powers to the HKMA shapes the bank's route into insurance.
Revocation and suspension of licences under s.81 are the sanctions that most affect the bank's distribution model.
Breaches of the conduct requirements are the most common basis for disciplinary action against intermediaries.
AML and CFT breaches can trigger separate disciplinary regimes, so both regimes must be managed together.
Complaints often feed into investigations, so complaint handling is part of the supervisory picture.

title: Complaints, cooling-off & policyholder protection
oneLiner: Customers reach the bank first, then the insurer, then industry bodies and the courts, and protection after an insurer fails is thinner than many customers assume.
keyPoints: **Own the complaint:** The bank should log, route and track every insurance complaint it receives, even where the insurer or agency makes the final decision.

**Escalation path:** Personal policy disputes usually run from the seller to the insurer, then to the Insurance Complaints Bureau (ICB) for policy-term or claims disputes, or to the Financial Dispute Resolution Centre (FDRC) for bank selling-process disputes (both reported), and then to the courts.

**Cooling-off:** IA guideline GL29 gives a cooling-off period of 21 calendar days for certain types of life insurance policies (its para 4.2 lists them; check the current text). It is a guideline under s.133, not law in itself. For general cover, check each policy's own cancellation terms.

**Insurer failure:** Long term assets sit in ring-fenced funds (s.21B), and a liquidator must carry on long term business with a view to a going concern transfer, unless the Court orders otherwise (s.46(2)). Most life and general policies have no compensation scheme in force.
**Void contracts:** A policy sold through a route the Ordinance does not allow can be voided at the policy holder's option, with premium refunded (s.64N(3)–(4)).
**Counsel's role:** Map each complaint route into the agency and partner agreements, and keep records that can be produced to the IA, the HKMA or the ICB.

deepDive.heading: Complaints inside the bank and the insurer
deepDive.lede: The first complaint usually lands with the bank, so the bank needs a clear handling route before the insurer is involved.
points: **Code of Conduct:** The Code of Conduct for Licensed Insurance Agents is published under s.95 and sets practice standards for licensed intermediaries. Breach does not by itself create liability (s.95(5)), but it can count against fitness to stay licensed (s.95(6)), and in proceedings under the Ordinance a court must take relevant provisions into account (s.95(7)).

**Who answers:** Where the bank sells as an appointed agent, s.68 makes the insurer answerable for the agent's dealings on issue or related business, even outside authority. Complaint handling may fall within that scope.

**Agency route:** If a licensed insurance agency or broker company sells the policy, that firm holds the licence and the conduct duties, and the agreement should say who answers which complaint and within what time. Where the bank itself is the agent, a regulatory complaint about its conduct goes to the HKMA (reported).
**Records:** A dated log of each complaint, product, outcome and reason is the first thing a reviewer will look at to judge the handling.
**Timing gap:** No regulatory response deadline for insurer complaints is stated here. Set internal targets, and check the Code text for any fixed period before publishing one.
deepDive.takeaway: Agree in writing who answers each complaint type, and keep one log that the bank, the agency and the insurer can all see.

deepDive.heading: The ICB and the FDRC
deepDive.lede: Two bodies handle most disputes after the firm has answered, but their remits differ and some figures are dated.
points: **ICB limit:** The ICB announced an increase in its monetary limit from HK$1.2m to HK$1.5m, effective 1 January 2025. Older material gives HK$1m, so confirm the current figure with the ICB before quoting it.
**ICB scope:** Reported exclusions include industrial, commercial and third-party insurance, and matters already in legal proceedings or arbitration.
**ICB process:** The ICB accepts written complaints and first refers the case to the insurer. A case the insurer still refuses goes to adjudication. Check the current procedure with the ICB.

**FDRC remit:** Bank disclosures say a bank must join the FDRC scheme for disputes about how an insurance product was sold. Disputes about a policy's terms or a claim go to the insurer first and then, for personal policies, to the ICB. These are bank statements, not FDRC rules: check the FDRC's current terms of reference.

**Appeals Tribunal:** The Insurance Appeals Tribunal reviews specified IA decisions on application by an affected person, within 21 days (s.100(1)). It is a regulatory review route, not a customer claims forum.
deepDive.takeaway: Tell customers which body fits their dispute, and never describe the Appeals Tribunal as a complaints channel.

deepDive.heading: Cooling-off and cancellation
deepDive.lede: A short free-look period is the customer's easiest exit, and it comes from guidance rather than from the Ordinance.
points: **GL29:** IA guideline GL29 gives a cooling-off period of 21 calendar days for certain types of life insurance policies (its para 4.2 lists them; check the current text). Some product sources say 30 days, so check GL29 itself before quoting either figure.
**Scope:** GL29 covers only the life policy types its para 4.2 lists (reported to exclude group policies). For general cover, check each policy's own cancellation terms before applying the period.

**Voidable contracts:** Under s.64N(3)–(4), a policy holder may choose to enforce or void a contract made in breach of the intermediary rule, and recover premium if it is voided before expiry. This is a separate route from cooling-off.
**Sales practice:** A customer who did not understand the cancellation right is a conduct issue for the bank, to be handled under stage 7.
deepDive.takeaway: Show the cancellation right and the refund route in the app at purchase and after issue, and make cancellation a single, logged step.

deepDive.heading: Insurer failure and policy holder protection
deepDive.lede: Protection depends on the class of business, and the schemes that exist cover only parts of the market.
points: **Ring-fencing:** s.21B requires separate funds for class C, G and H business and for specified business. Under s.23(1), assets in a fund may be applied only for that part of the business.
**Liquidation:** Under s.46(2), a liquidator carries on the long term business with a view to a going concern transfer, but may not enter new contracts. The court may reduce contracts (s.46(5)).

**Motor and employees' compensation:** Two industry schemes cover insurer failure in compulsory classes. The Motor Insurers' Bureau pays victims where the at-fault driver is uninsured or untraceable, or the insurer has failed (reported). The Employees Compensation Insurer Insolvency Bureau, set up by the industry in 2003, runs a scheme in force since 1 April 2004 that meets employees' compensation claims when an insurer becomes insolvent; it took over Target Insurance's employees' compensation policies after the winding-up petition of 15 July 2022.

**Proposed scheme:** The government published conclusions on 28 December 2023 for a statutory Policyholders' Protection Scheme. Reported payout options were HK$1m, HK$2m or HK$4m per policy. No enacted law or 2025 or 2026 timetable is reported.
**Gap:** No equivalent scheme is reported in force for life or most general policies, so disclosure should say so rather than imply cover.
deepDive.takeaway: Tell customers which protection applies to their product, and do not describe the proposed scheme as in force.

deepDive.heading: Civil liability
deepDive.lede: Courts decide what a customer can recover, and the liability of the insurer and the bank can overlap on one sale.
points: **Agent liability:** Where one authorized insurer appoints the agent, the insurer is liable for the agent's acts in dealings about issue or related business, even outside authority (s.68(2)). It is not liable if the agent clearly disclosed the lack of authority before the client relied on the act (s.68(4C)). Where several insurers appoint the agent, s.68(3)–(4B) allocate liability by line of business and scope of authority.
**Void contracts:** Where a policy is voided under s.64N(3)(b), the policy holder recovers the consideration paid (s.64N(4)). Refund exposure should be reflected in the agency terms.
**Offence:** An authorized insurer that contravenes s.64N(1) or (2) commits an offence, with a maximum fine of HK$1m and two years' imprisonment on indictment (s.64N(5)(a)).

**Bank's own exposure:** The bank may face claims in its own right for poor advice or misrepresentation in the sale. This stage does not set out the general contract or tort principles, which need a case law check before advice is given.

**Codes as evidence:** In proceedings under the Ordinance, a code is admissible, and the court must take account of relevant provisions (s.95(7)). Breach does not by itself create liability (s.95(5)), but it can count against fitness to stay licensed (s.95(6)).
deepDive.takeaway: Assume the insurer and the bank can both be exposed over one sale, and document each party's role in it.

provisions.title: Authorized insurer’s relationship with its agent
provisions.summary: An authorized insurer is liable for acts of its appointed agent in dealings for the issue of a policy or related insurance business, even if outside the agent's authority, unless the agent clearly disclosed the lack of authority before the client relied on the act (s.68(4C)). Where several insurers appoint the agent, subsections (3) to (4B) allocate liability by line of business and scope of authority. The court may weigh other factors (s.68(4D)).
provisions.counselNote: Set out the bank's agency role in writing, and align complaint handling with the insurer so that each act is clearly within the mandate. The insurer carries the liability, which supports tight oversight of the bank's conduct.

provisions.title: Contracts of insurance entered into in contravention of section 6(1)
provisions.summary: Where an insurer enters a contract in contravention of s.6(1), the policy holder may choose either to enforce it or to void it. A policy holder who voids before expiry recovers the consideration paid.
provisions.counselNote: Before showing a product, confirm the insurer is authorized for that class. A contract written by an unauthorized insurer can be voided by the customer, so the bank carries the reputational and refund exposure.

provisions.title: Contracts of insurance made through persons other than licensed insurance intermediaries, etc.
provisions.summary: An authorized insurer must not contract through a person in Hong Kong unless that person is a licensed agency, a licensed individual agent appointed by the insurer, a licensed broker company, or a person doing only clerical work. A breach allows the policy holder to enforce or void the contract, and is an offence.
provisions.counselNote: This is the main reason the bank's route into insurance must be correct before any complaint arises. Confirm in stages 3 and 4 which route the bank uses, and whether it is covered by the licensing position.

provisions.title: Maintenance of separate accounts and funds in respect of long term business
provisions.summary: Insurers with long term business must keep separate accounts and funds for class C, G and H business and for specified business. Participating business must sit in a separate sub-fund within the specified business fund. Section 23(1) then limits the use of those assets to their own part of the business.
provisions.counselNote: Explain to customers that long term assets are ring-fenced, but that this is a feature of the insurer's balance sheet, not a guarantee of payment. The bank should not describe it as deposit-style protection.

provisions.title: Continuation of long term business of authorized insurer in liquidation
provisions.summary: On winding up of an insurer with long term business, the liquidator carries on that business with a view to transferring it as a going concern and may not enter new contracts. The court may reduce the amount of existing contracts on conditions.
provisions.counselNote: A failed insurer's policies may be moved to another insurer rather than paid out. The bank's partner list and any customer communications should reflect that a transfer is the statutory aim unless the Court orders otherwise, and that the Court may reduce contracts instead (s.46(5)).

provisions.title: Insurance Appeals Tribunal
provisions.summary: The Tribunal reviews specified decisions made by the IA, on application by an affected person made within 21 days of notice of the decision. It is a regulatory review body and does not decide customer claims against insurers or agents.
provisions.counselNote: Do not present the Tribunal as a complaints route for customers. Its relevance to the bank is as a review forum for the specified IA decisions listed in Sch. 9. Check Sch. 9 before naming any licence or approval decision as reviewable.

provisions.title: Codes of conduct for licensed insurance intermediaries
provisions.summary: The IA may publish codes of conduct for licensed insurance intermediaries. Breach does not by itself create liability, but the code may count against fitness to stay licensed, and the court must take account of relevant provisions in any proceedings under the Ordinance.
provisions.counselNote: Treat the Code as binding in practice. Its complaint standards will be used as the benchmark when a complaint is reviewed, so the bank's procedure should match them.

provisions.instrument: Code of Conduct for Licensed Insurance Agents (IA)
provisions.ref: Code of Conduct for Licensed Insurance Agents
provisions.title: Code of Conduct for Licensed Insurance Agents
provisions.summary: Issued under s.95, with a first edition effective 23 September 2019. It sets practice standards for licensed agents. The complaint-handling paragraphs need checking against the current text, and the IA may handle conduct complaints about intermediaries. Complaints about banks acting as intermediaries are reported to go to the HKMA under the 2019 IA-HKMA memorandum.
provisions.counselNote: Read the complaint section of the current Code before writing the bank's procedure. The HKMA routing is reported; check it with the HKMA.

provisions.title: Guideline on Cooling-off Period
provisions.summary: GL29 gives a cooling-off period of 21 calendar days for certain types of life insurance policies, to cancel for a premium refund (its para 4.2 lists them; check the current text). Some product sources cite 30 days. It is a guideline under s.133, not law in itself.
provisions.counselNote: Build the period into the app from the GL29 text, not from product summaries. For general cover, check each policy's own cancellation terms. The period runs 21 calendar days from delivery of the policy or a Cooling-off Notice, whichever is earlier (reported; check GL29).

provisions.title: Insurance Complaints Bureau: personal insurance disputes
provisions.summary: The ICB is an industry body that handles disputes over personal insurance, up to a monetary limit. The limit was reported as increased from HK$1.2m to HK$1.5m from 1 January 2025. Commercial, industrial and third-party disputes and matters in legal proceedings are reported as excluded.
provisions.counselNote: Give customers the current limit from the ICB, and tell them that the ICB handles the insurer's decision rather than the bank's selling practice. Keep the referral wording under review.

provisions.instrument: Financial Dispute Resolution Centre (FDRC) terms of reference
provisions.title: Financial Dispute Resolution Centre: intake for bank-related disputes
provisions.summary: The FDRC is reported to handle disputes with a bank about the selling process of an insurance product, while disputes over policy terms go to the ICB. Its published material dates from 2014 to 2017, and reform proposals to widen the scheme are reported (check their status).
provisions.counselNote: Confirm the current terms of reference before telling a customer that the FDRC covers a bank-sold policy. Bank disclosures say a bank must join the FDRC scheme for selling-process disputes. Confirm this against the FDRC's own terms before relying on it.

provisions.title: Policyholders' Protection Scheme (proposed)
provisions.summary: The government published consultation conclusions on 28 December 2023 for a statutory scheme to protect policy holders when an insurer fails. The December 2022 consultation proposed per-policy payout options of HK$1m, HK$2m or HK$4m (reported). Check the final design and its legislative status. No enacted law or timetable for 2025 or 2026 is reported.
provisions.counselNote: Describe the scheme only as proposed. Check its status with the Financial Services and the Treasury Bureau and the IA before any customer communication refers to it.

checklist: **Complaint route map:** Write the path for each product, from the bank to the agency, the insurer, the ICB, the FDRC and the courts.
**Single complaint log:** Record date, product, channel, outcome and time to answer, and share it with partners under the agency terms.
**Partner agreements:** Set who answers each complaint type, handover times and cooperation on ICB and FDRC files.
**ICB and FDRC scripts:** Give customers the correct body and the current limit, and check the figures before publishing them.
**Cooling-off in the app:** Show the period and refund route at purchase and after issue, and confirm the period and exemptions against GL29.
**Insurer status check:** Confirm each insurer is authorized for the class before a product is shown, to limit s.6A and s.64N exposure.
**Protection disclosure:** State which compensation or fund protections apply to each product, and say when a proposed scheme is not yet law.
**Record retention:** Keep complaint and cancellation files for an agreed period, in a form that can be produced to the IA, the HKMA or the ICB.
itAngle: **Complaint tooling:** Build a case record that carries the product, policy number, channel, dates and the partner that owns the answer.
**Cancellation flow:** Make cooling-off cancellation a self-service step, with refund status and a confirmation, all logged against the policy.
**Sale journey records:** Keep a retrievable record of the sale (screens, disclosures and timestamps), since a complaint review will start from it.
**Insurer status feed:** Track insurer authorization and financial-status changes so the app can stop selling a product when its insurer is in difficulty.
bankNotes: **Bank owns the relationship:** Customers expect the bank to take their complaint, even where the insurer decides the claim. Route it quickly and tell the customer who makes the decision.
**Agent position:** Where the bank is an appointed agent, s.68 makes the insurer answerable for the bank's dealings, which gives both parties a reason to align complaint handling.

**Two complaint tracks (reported):** A regulatory complaint about the bank's conduct as an agency goes to the HKMA under the 2019 IA-HKMA memorandum. A money claim over the sale goes to the FDRC (reported from bank disclosures), and a personal policy-term or claims dispute to the ICB. Confirm the routing with both bodies.
**Partner terms:** Put complaint cooperation, data sharing and cost sharing into the agency or insurer agreement, and check the data terms against stage 9.
pitfalls: **Quoting a stale ICB limit:** Sources differ on the figure, so publish only the current limit from the ICB.
**Treating the Appeals Tribunal as a complaints route:** It reviews specified IA decisions, not customer claims against insurers or agents.
**Assuming a protection scheme exists:** The motor and employees' compensation arrangements are the only ones found in force, and the Policyholders' Protection Scheme is proposed only.
**Assuming one cooling-off period:** Sources disagree between 21 and 30 days, and exemptions vary, so take the period from GL29 for each life product and check each general policy's own terms.

glossary.definition: Industry body that handles disputes over personal insurance after the insurer has given its decision, up to a monetary limit. Its decisions bind the insurer rather than the customer (reported).
Dispute body for disputes with banks and other regulated financial institutions. Reported to cover selling-process disputes involving a bank, while policy-term disputes go to the ICB.
Short period after purchase in which a life policy holder may cancel for a premium refund. It comes from an IA guideline (GL29), not from the Ordinance.
Tribunal under Cap. 41, Part XII, that reviews specified IA decisions on application by an affected person (s.100).
Separate fund holding assets for part of an insurer's long term business, which may be applied only for that part (ss.21B and 23).
Transfer of an insurer's business as a running whole to another insurer, rather than closing contracts one by one (s.46).
Proposed statutory scheme to protect policy holders when an insurer fails. Announced by government in December 2023 and not reported as in force.
Industry bureau that pays motor accident victims where the at-fault driver is uninsured or untraceable, or the insurer has failed. Funded by motor premium levies (reported).

Industry bureau set up in 2003 that meets employees' compensation claims when an insurer becomes insolvent. In force since 1 April 2004, and took over Target Insurance's employees' compensation policies (reported).

related.why: Sales practices behind many complaints, and the best-interests duty that a complaint review will test.
Licence status of the bank, agencies and individuals determines whether a contract can be voided under s.64N.
The bank's chosen route into insurance decides who answers a complaint.
Complaint records and how they are reported to the IA and HKMA.
Records of the digital sale journey are the main evidence in any complaint review.
